#8622. Wildfires Force Closure of Carstenz Pyramid for the Season

All around the world, natural disasters are hampering climbing expeditions. The latest case is a series of uncontrolled wildfires in Papua that have doomed the fall climbing season on Carstenz Pyramid.

The region is facing severe, widespread forest fires that have blanketed the island in a persistent thick haze. The air quality and visibility have reached levels that make transportation, logistics, and climbing operations impossible, according to local outfitter Tropic Adventure Papua. Apparently, the effects of the El Niño phenomenon, known this year as the Super Niño due to its extraordinary intensity, are to blame. It has brought a prolonged drought and extremely dry air, diminishing hope for the rain needed to extinguish the fires.

By the time the situation became unbearable, the first groups of foreign climbers had reached Timika in Papua, but no one made it to the top during this season, which is now officially canceled.

Outfitters have already shared the news with their clients and are now placing their hopes in 2027.

“Our thoughts are with the local communities affected, and we’re hoping the fires are brought under control soon,” Garrett Madison posted on social media. Instead, they have set the dates for next year, with two trips in March and October.

Tragically, the situation in Papua is only a fraction of a major environmental catastrophe. Wildfires are sweeping through the Indonesian archipelago and affecting Malaysia and Singapore:

The harm caused to the fragile Indonesian ecosystem is incalculable. In recent days, a viral video of a young orangutan rescued from a treetop where it tried to escape with burned hands and feet has drawn attention to the disaster. In fact, a significant number of primates were evacuated by rescue services in Borneo. Some of them were returned to the forests as the fire receded last weekend, according to the BBC.

The intensity of the fires in Papua and the air quality can be tracked live here.

At 4,884m, Carstenz Pyramid (Puncak Jaya in the local language) is the highest point of Oceania and considered one of the Seven Summits. Located in Central Papua, and with a tropical climate, Carstenz can be climbed at any time of year. However, summit options increase in the less rainy months, from February through November.

Outfitters apply for permits twice a year. Political unrest has often kept climbers away in the past, and major mining operations limit ground access. Climbers are typically airlifted to Base Camp instead of trekking through the jungle.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

Do you think a million-dollar term life insurance policy sounds like too much insurance?

As a Certified Financial Planner, I see underinsured people every day.

A million-dollar term life insurance policy might actually be the minimum coverage needed for the typical middle-class household, but it’s affordable.

That might sound like an exaggeration, but if you crunch the numbers – just as we’ll be doing a little bit – you’ll realize that a million-dollar policy might be just what you need.

The good news is term life insurance isn’t nearly as costly as most people think.

What makes term life insurance even better is that larger policies cost less on a per thousand basis than smaller policies do. You may find the premium on a $1 million policy is only a little bit higher than it is for $500,000.

Probably, but let’s find out. A general rule of thumb is that you should get 10x your income as baseline coverage for life insurance.

If you’re young, that may be low because you may want to provide your family with enough to replace your income for 15 years or more.

Today, $1 million has become the new baseline for life insurance by a primary breadwinner. Anything less could leave your family financially impaired.

Here’s a list of all the different obligations you may want to have life insurance cover in the unfortunate event you pass away early.

Now that you have an idea of these obligations, let’s punch them into this life insurance calculator to find out if you need a million-dollar policy.

According to Policy Genius, the average cost for a 20-year $1 million term life insurance policy for a 35-year-old male is $53 per month. However, your rate will vary according to the following factors.

The best, and easiest place to start is online. I recommend having two or three insurers compete for your business to make sure you get the best rate and coverage. To see how cheap term life can be, choose your state from the map above to be matched with top life insurance providers instantly.

Let’s look at the individual components that can quickly add up to over a million-dollar policy.

This is where things can get a bit intimidating. Even if you earn a modest income, you may need close to $1 million to replace that income after your death in order to provide for your family’s basic living expenses.

The conventional wisdom in the insurance industry is that you should maintain a life insurance policy equal to between 10 times and 20 times your annual income. So if you earn around $50K per year, that would mean policy coverage between $500K and $1 million.

The complication today is that with interest rates being as low as they are that might not be enough either.

For example, if you have a $1 million policy that could be invested at 5% per year, your family could live on the interest earned – which conveniently comes to $50,000 per year – for the next 20 years.

That would still leave the original $1 million intact to cover other expenses. But with today’s microscopic interest rates, there’s no way to get a guaranteed return of 5% on your money, certainly not for 15 or 20 years.

Also, keep in mind that most insurance companies have a maximum multiplier you can apply to your income for life insurance coverage. For example, it wouldn’t make much sense for a 22-year-old making $27,000 per year to get a $2 million life insurance. Or a 65-year-old that is retired to secure a $3 million dollar policy.

The table below is approximately how much you’re allowed to multiply your income based on your age and income:

Using the table above as a guide, a 35-year-old making $150,000 per year would be capped at taking out a $4.5 million term policy ($150,000 x 30 = $4,500,000).

Here we start with the basics – wrapping up your final affairs.

This will include funeral costs and any lingering medical costs. A reasonable estimate for a typical funeral is around $20,000.

Crazy, right? You can get burial insurance to cover only the most basic of final expenses.

Debt burdens are high in the US, and debt can be especially crushing on remaining family members. Many life insurance customers make sure they can pay off most of their debt with the policy.

Medical costs are a serious variable. Even if you have excellent health insurance, there are likely to be unpaid medical bills lingering after your death. This has to do with copayments, deductibles, and coinsurance provisions.

Collectively, they can add up to many thousands of dollars. But where things get really complicated is if you die of a terminal illness.

For example, if you are stricken by an illness that lasts for several years, you could incur a number of expenses that are not covered by insurance. This may include the cost of personal care and even experimental treatments.

A home may be a large asset, but it’s also often a homeowner’s largest debt. The average mortgage balance in the US is roughly $236,443 according to Experian data. So you could easily use a life insurance policy to pay off that debt and relieve your loved ones of a monthly mortgage payment.

Credit card debt and other personal debt are some of the most expensive obligations carrying rates upward of 20% in some cases. Make sure you have enough to cover this very expensive debt.

Below is a sampling of major expenses your family is likely to incur, either on an annual basis or at some point after your death.

Tuition costs continue to skyrocket. The Department of Education suggests that four-year public college tuition has been rising an average of 5% per year, far exceeding the rate of inflation. If you have one child who attends an in-state public school, a second at an out-of-state public school, and a third in a private university, the total expenditure will reach $416,560.

Vehicles and other forms of transportation represent another large sum. Unfortunately, with increasing electronics and safety features, the average cost of a new car continues to grow.

If your family relies on your work for healthcare, take notice. According to eHealth.com, the average health insurance premium for a family is $22,221. That’s a shade under $2,000 per month in additional cost. This cost will only rise, and the need could last for years.

So far, we’ve been describing the financial obligations likely to affect a typical household.But there may be certain situations that will produce obligations that are less obvious.

For example, if you’re a business owner, there may be debts or other financial obligations that will need to be paid upon your death.

Even though no one in your family may be qualified or interested in taking over your business, the payoff of those obligations may be completely necessary to enable the sale of the business.

Another possibility is that you’re a real estate investor.

If your properties are heavily indebted, extra insurance proceeds may be necessary either to carry the properties until they’re sold, or even to pay off existing indebtedness to free up cash flow for income.

You may even need additional funds if you are taking care of an extended family member, like an aging parent.

These are just some of the many possibilities of expenses that will need to be covered by insurance proceeds.

Before we move on to specific life insurance quotes, let’s first consider the factors that affect term life insurance premiums.

This is typically the single most important premium factor. The older you are, the more likely you are to die within the term of the policy.

This is a close second and why it’s so important to apply for a policy as early in life as possible. Premiums on life insurances rates literally increase by each year.

If you have any health conditions that may affect mortality, such as diabetes or hypertension, your premiums will be higher. This is another compelling reason to apply while you are young and in good health.

It’s not that policies are not available to people with health conditions, it’s just that they’re less expensive if you don’t have any.

A 10-year term policy will have a lower premium than a 20-year term policy, which will be lower than a 30-year term. The shorter the term, the less likely it is the insurance company will have to pay a claim before it expires.

Size of the policy matters, but not the way you might think. Yes, a $1 million policy will cost more than a $500,000 policy. But it won’t cost twice as much.

The larger the policy, the lower the per-thousand cost will be.

When the size of the death benefit is considered, the larger policy will always be more cost-effective.

For example, certain occupations are more hazardous than others (think policeman versus librarian). Deep-sea diving is higher risk than golf. And smoking is the one activity guaranteed to raise your premiums substantially.

With this information in mind, let’s take a look at whether you should consider a $1 million whole life policy instead.

Any discussion on life insurance should include a comparison of whole life and term life insurance coverage. After all, both products can be immensely valuable in the right situation, yet one product (whole life) costs considerably more than the other.

Most of the time, the debate is settled in favor of term life insurance based on cost alone.

A whole life insurance policy can easily cost 10x the same amount of coverage you can get with a term policy.

With that being said, whole life insurance and other investment-type life insurance coverage can be valuable in terms of the cash value you can build up over time. Whole life insurance also offers a fixed benefit amount for your heirs that will last for your entire life, yet the cost of your premiums are guaranteed to stay the same.

The cash value of a whole life insurance policy also grows on a tax-deferred basis, and you can borrow against this amount if you need a loan. Further, many whole life policies from reputable providers also pay out dividends during good years, which can be substantial.

The problem with whole life and other similar policies like universal life is the fact that premiums can be exorbitant for the amount of coverage you might need.

A couple with young children provides a good example since they might need a $1 million dollar policy or more to provide income protection for their working years and have money left for college tuition and other expenses.

With young families, expenses are already high.

This includes costs for food for a family, childcare, heavy use of health care, and the seemingly endless demand for clothing, furniture, and even entertainment as the children grow.

As you can see from the cost comparison below from State Farm, there’s not enough room in the typical family budget to afford the type of life insurance that’s needed.

A 40-year-old mother and breadwinner in excellent health would pay $80.09 per month for a term life policy that lasts 20 years, whereas a whole life policy in the same amount would cost $1,266.69 per month (or $14,560 annually).

This is a classic situation where term insurance rides to the rescue. The family can afford to buy the amount of coverage they need at an affordable price, whereas paying for permanent life insurance coverage in the same amount would be difficult to justify.

And just as important for people of any age and in any circumstance, the extra funds not being spent on insurance premiums can be invested to gradually improve your financial situation.

So absolutely, term insurance will work best for most people.

As you’ll notice, each table has a wide array of information. Knowing that everybody is in a different situation, I wanted to make sure that I offered term life quotes for almost every conceivable situation.

I’ve included life insurance rates for a 30-year term, 20-year term, and a 10-year term million dollar life policies. If you’re a tobacco user, I’ve also included some quotes from life insurance for smokers.

For those that think that a million-dollar term policy is expensive, you’ll quickly notice that a 25-year-old male in good health only costs $645 per year while a 35-year-old costs $795.

On a monthly basis that’s almost next to nothing!

There is a big drop-off in life insurance rates between a 20 year and a 30 year since underwriters do not have to worry as much about life expectancy.

For many people, a 20-year policy gets them exactly where they want to be in life when the policy term runs out.

Once again, you get a $200 drop in the annual premium by losing another 10 years on the term.

If your life insurance agent isn’t giving you all these term options and is only focused on the death benefit, then you need a different agent.

For all you smokers out there – beware! The cost of your life insurance balloons as you’ll see here. If you’re considering kicking the habit, now is as good time as any.

Some life insurance companies will give you a lower rate if you complete a recognized smoking cessation program, and go on without smoking for at least two years.

It won’t help your immediate situation, but when you see the premium on smoker life insurance rates below, you might agree that it’s something to work toward!

If you’ve made the decision that $1 million of life insurance is the right amount of coverage you need and you’re ready to purchase a policy, here are the steps you’ll need to follow.

1. Determine How Much Coverage You Need: This is the first and most important step in securing a million life insurance policies. You need to have a clear understanding of how much coverage you actually need.

2. Choose the Right Type of Policy: There are whole life, term life, and Universal life policies available. Choose the one that best suits your needs.

3. Shop Around: Don’t just go with the first life insurance company you come across. It’s important to compare life insurance rates and coverage from a few different companies before making a decision.

4. Consider Your Health: If you’re in good health, you’ll likely qualify for lower rates. However, if you have health issues, you may still be able to get coverage, but it will probably be more expensive.

5. Consider Your Lifestyle: If you have a risky job or hobby, that could affect your rates.

6. Get Quotes From Multiple Companies: This is the best way to compare rates and find the cheapest policy.

7. Read the Fine Print: Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions of the policy before buying it.

8. Buy Online: You can usually get cheaper rates by buying life insurance online.

9. Pay Attention to Your Payment Schedule: Most life insurance policies require monthly or annual payments. Be sure you can afford the payments before buying a policy.

10. Review Your Policy Regularly: Life changes, and so do life insurance needs. Be sure to review your policy regularly to make sure it still meets your needs.

Following these steps will help you get the best possible rate on a million-dollar life insurance policy.

Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions before signing on the dotted line. Also, make sure to shop around and compare rates from multiple companies before buying a policy.

Yes, I know I’ve said that a few times in this article, but it’s worth repeating. Many people go with the first life insurance company they call, and that isn’t kind to their checkbook. It pays to shop around.

Here’s what you need to know about choosing the best life insurance company for your $1 million policy:

When choosing the best life insurance company, it’s important to consider the overall financial health of the insurance company. You want to make sure the company you choose is stable and will be around for years to come. You also want to consider things like the company’s customer service rating and claims-paying ability.

There are a lot of different life insurance companies out there, so it can be difficult to know which one is the best. Each company is rated by different organizations, so it’s important to look at multiple ratings before making a decision.

Rating agencies are the “Report Card” for life insurance companies. Choose a company with straight A’s!

The companies that rate insurance companies are A.M. Best, Moody’s, and Standard & Poor’s.

A.M. Best is a credit rating agency that specializes in the insurance industry. They rate insurance companies on their financial stability.

Moody’s is another credit rating agency. They also rate insurance companies on their financial stability.

Standard & Poor’s is a credit rating agency that rates companies on their financial stability.

The following life insurance companies are all rated A+ (Superior) by A.M. Best and are considered to be financially stable and have a good claim-paying ability.

When choosing a life insurance company, it’s important to consider their financial stability, customer service rating, and claims-paying ability. The companies listed above are all rated A+ (Superior) by A.M. Best and are considered to be financially stable with a good claims-paying ability.

Northwestern Mutual, New York Life, MassMutual, Guardian Life, State Farm, Nationwide, USAA, MetLife, The Hartford, and Allstate are all good choices for life insurance companies.

You can’t put a price on peace of mind, and with a $1 million life insurance policy you can have the peace of mind knowing that your loved ones will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

Getting a one-million-dollar term life insurance policy is not as expensive as most people believe. You can start getting quotes today from a variety of top life insurers by selecting your state from the map above.

Even those who opt for the more expensive permanent life insurance policy will many times be surprised at the price.

Either way, you can get these larger amounts of coverage and still not break the bank. But get your policy now, while you’re still young and in good health.

The cost of a $1,000,000 life insurance policy will vary based on factors like your age, health, and lifestyle. However, you can expect to pay around $250 per year for a healthy 30-year-old. According to Ladder Life, a $1 million term life policy for healthy 30-year-old males costs around $2.08 per day.

A $1 million term life insurance policy is a type of life insurance that provides coverage for a specific period of time, usually 10-20 years. If you die during the term of the policy, your beneficiaries will receive a death benefit of $1 million. If you live past the term of the policy, the policy will expire and you will not receive any death benefit. A $1 million term life insurance policy is a good choice for people who want to make sure their loved ones are taken care of financially if something happens to them. It can also be a good choice for people with a lot of debt, like a mortgage or student loans, that they want to make sure is paid off if they die.

For the most part, yes; but there are examples of people who cannot buy life insurance. For instance, people with a terminal illness or those who have been diagnosed with a life expectancy of fewer than two years are not able to purchase life insurance policies. The other factors are your income, affordability, and suitability. If you cannot afford the premiums, then you will not be able to purchase the policy. And if your income is say less than $50,000 then the insurance company may not think it’s suitable to purchase a $1 million life insurance policy.

A million-dollar life insurance policy may not be right for everyone, but it can be a good idea if you have a lot of debt or if you want to make sure your family is taken care of financially if something happens to you. No one likes to think about their death, but it’s important to have a life insurance policy in place in case something happens to you. A million-dollar life insurance policy can give you and your loved one’s peace of mind knowing that they will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

There is no one-size-fits-all answer to this question, as the best policy for you will depend on your specific needs and preferences. However, some of the top providers of million-dollar life insurance policies include AIG, Banner Life, and Prudential. So be sure to explore your options and compare quotes from different providers before making a decision.

#8620. Teens Can Invest Before 18 – Ask a Parent to Open a Custodial Account

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

You can’t open a brokerage account alone until you’re an adult, but a parent can set up a custodial account for you now, or a custodial Roth IRA once you earn money from work. Put your first dollars into one broad index fund and leave them alone, since money invested as a teen gets the most years to grow.

Which account a parent opens decides who makes the trades until you’re an adult. Ask for a custodial account if you’re happy to let your parent pick the investments, or a teen account if you’d rather pick them yourself.

In a custodial account, often called a UTMA or UGMA account after the state laws behind it, the money is legally yours from the first deposit. Your parent manages it as custodian until the age your state sets, usually 18 or 21, when you take over.

Teen accounts like the Fidelity Youth Account and the Schwab Teen Investor account, both for ages 13 to 17, let you place the trades while a parent can see each one. Fidelity’s account belongs to you alone, and your parent, who must already have a Fidelity account, can’t trade in it. Schwab’s is a joint account you share with your parent, who can trade and withdraw too. At 18, you can move either one into a regular account in your own name.

Once you earn money from work, a parent can also open a custodial Roth IRA for you, where the growth can come out tax-free in retirement.

Whichever account you use, start with one broad index fund, a fund that owns the stocks in a market index, such as the 500 large U.S. companies in the S&P 500. One purchase spreads your money across all of them, so you don’t have to guess which ones will do well. If you’re curious about picking stocks, try it with a small part of your money, such as $100 of every $1,000.

Then leave the money alone. At a hypothetical 7% average yearly return before inflation, with nothing added or taken out, $2,000 invested at 16 grows to about $30,000 by 56. That $30,000 is about $10,000 more than the $20,000 the same $2,000 reaches when invested at 22.

Pick the account with a parent this week, and use your first deposit to buy the index fund as soon as it arrives.

Before a parent opens your custodial account, compare the best custodial accounts for kids.

#8619. Russians Give Up on the Khumbu Icefall; Will Try Everest West Ridge Instead

The first steps on a lonely Everest were daunting for four Russian climbers, who tried and failed to cross the Khumbu Icefall. They adapted quickly, heading up to the Lho La instead and setting up camp at that high pass at the base of the West Ridge.

Andrei Vasiliev, Natalya Belyankina, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Valery Sipilov set off from Lobuche on their first round up the mountain last week. Their original plan was to attempt the Khumbu Icefall, which has no ladders or ropes at this time of year. They set off at 5 am on October 9, looking for a way through the maze of seracs and crevasses.

“At first glance, it appears to be pure, unadulterated chaos,” Sergey Kondrashkin later wrote. “Yet on closer inspection, one can discern distinct sections. We opted for the central section, which seemed somewhat more solid — though ‘solid is a relative term…At least, it was easier to envision a viable path here between the seracs, snowfields, and ice walls.”

The recent snowy spell that hit Nepal filled many of the crevasses but also had a downside: loads of hard trail-breaking through deep snow.

Kondrashkin reported they crossed the most difficult terrain with only a few ropes in some sections and mostly moved as a roped team of four. “Time and again, I broke through the surface, sinking in up to my waist or even my chest,” he wrote. “By the end of the day, we reached an altitude of 5,700m, with still 500 vertical meters to go to the top of the Icefall and the biggest crevasses on the upper part.” They planted their tent on a small, flat platform.

“Conditions did not improve on the following morning,” Natalya Belyankina reported. “We ran out of steam on the second day, having gained only 100m in elevation after six hours, so we decided to head back down.”

The Russian team in the Khumbu Icefall on Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

However, they had food for four days, so instead of returning to Lobuche, they retraced their steps across the Icefall in three hours (they had spent one day and a half going up) and pitched the tent right below the high pass known as Lho La.

That was their second potential route. The Lho La is the col between Khumbutse, a lesser peak that rises to the left, and the characteristic pyramidal peak known as Everest’s West Shoulder. Lying on the border between Nepal and Tibet, it gives access to the very long West Ridge to the summit. It is also the route that Jost Kobusch will attempt in two months’ time. The German is on his fourth attempt to solo Everest in winter.

The Russian team’s tent in front of the wall leading to the Lho La between Nepal and Tibet. Photo: Natalya Belyankina/Instagram

Progress up the Lho La was fast, unlike the Icefall. The team completed the mixed terrain of the 600m wall in a single day, then pitched their tent on the col. On the fourth day, they scouted the terrain above and went to the base of the West Ridge, before returning to Lobuche for now, Alpymon reported.

The Russian team on a lonely Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

The climbers loved the experience of being completely alone on Everest. “Groups of trekkers only make it as far as that famous rock — joking, laughing, and congratulating one another,” Belyankina recalled. “Just yesterday, near the Everest Base Camp rock, a young man was playing the saxophone. It sounded wonderful. But once we cross a couple of moraines, that’s it — we’re all alone on the mountain.”

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

Your 40s still give new savings time to compound, so check now whether you’re on track for retirement. Fidelity’s guideline is to have at least three times your salary saved by 40 and six times by 50. Push your 401(k) contributions toward the yearly limit, fund an IRA, and start adding some bonds to your investments.

Find a retirement shortfall at 45, and you have about 20 years to close it before 65. Find it at 60, and you have five.

At a hypothetical 7% average annual return, $150,000 saved at 45 plus $1,000 a month grows to about $1.1 million by 65. Starting the $1,000 a month at 45 rather than 50 means five more years of deposits, $60,000 in all, and about $200,000 more at 65.

So divide your retirement savings by your salary now and compare the result with Fidelity’s guideline. It assumes you’ve saved 15% of your pay since age 25, any employer match included, and will retire at 67. The total to aim for is your retirement number, about 25 times the yearly spending Social Security won’t cover.

Whatever your numbers show, make these moves this decade:

If you’re behind, also plan to work a few years longer. Each extra year of work adds a year of saving and leaves one less year of retirement for your savings to pay for.

Log in to your 401(k) this week and raise your contribution by two percentage points, then add a point with every raise until you hit the limit.

#8616. Canada Coast to Coast Paddlers Begin Final Stretch

Canadian paddlers Will Vyse and Nolan Aziz — reduced to a twosome after Georges Kirijian left the expedition with an injury — are entering the final stretch of their mammoth 8,000km expedition from Tadoussac, Quebec, to Vancouver, British Columbia, on the Pacific Ocean.

After 184 days, including 34 days in Alberta, they crossed into British Columbia on October 10. This marks the final province of their trip. They have recently been paddling up the Peace River, which they describe as “long and arduous.”  The canoeists have covered well over 6,000km, and both they and their gear look suitably disheveled:

Once they finish with the Peace River, they have a meaty 17km portage to Williston Lake, the largest lake in British Columbia, before taking the southern branch of the Crooked River. After crossing the Continental Divide and completing the Giscome Portage between Summit Lake and the Fraser River, they will take the Fraser through Prince George and down to Vancouver.

Vyse and Aziz originally planned to end their trip in the town of Prince Rupert, but have since altered their route to finish at Vancouver’s Wreck Beach.

“Our reroute maintains a total expedition distance of over 8,000km, and upon completion will still be the longest ever recorded single-season canoe trip,” Vyse and Aziz wrote on social media.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8615. Avianca LifeMiles → Star Alliance Premium Cabin

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

One of the cheapest ways to fly Star Alliance business and first class

Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you. New York to Frankfurt — a route that commands $4,000 to $8,000 in cash for a business class ticket — and you're here for 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles. No fuel surcharges. No carrier-imposed fees eating into your redemption. Just the experience. That's the moment the FI community lives for. Not the luxury itself — though Lufthansa's business class product is genuinely exceptional — but the *math*. The realization that the loyalty system has a pricing gap so wide you could fly a 747 through it. Here's what the numbers actually mean. At the low end, a $4,000 business class ticket redeemed for 63,000 points works out to **6.3 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — peak travel season, last-minute pricing, transatlantic demand — that same seat hits $8,000 in cash, which means your LifeMiles are delivering **12.7 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1–2 CPP a baseline for points value. You're achieving 6 to 12 times that baseline. The reason this feels like a genuine inefficiency rather than just a deal: Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards on a **fixed award chart** that doesn't fluctuate with cash fare demand. When airlines raise transatlantic business class fares during summer holidays or major events, your points cost stays exactly the same. The gap between what the market charges and what LifeMiles charges simply grows wider. And then there's the no-fuel-surcharge policy — the detail that separates LifeMiles from competitors like British Airways Avios, which can pile $600+ in carrier surcharges onto a single redemption. With LifeMiles, you pay government taxes only, typically $50–$150 for a transatlantic itinerary. That's it. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents exactly the kind of asymmetric value that underpins a great travel rewards strategy: use points where cash prices are highest, eliminate fees wherever possible, and fly a product you'd never justify paying full price for — because you didn't have to.

The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program quickly enough to actually use them.

Avianca is a Star Alliance member, which means it has reciprocal award booking agreements with every other Star Alliance carrier — United, Lufthansa, Swiss, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines, and more. Like all alliance programs, LifeMiles can sell award seats on partner airlines. The pricing is set by Avianca's own award chart, not by Lufthansa's chart or United's chart.

This is the pricing inefficiency. Lufthansa's own frequent flyer program (Miles & More) charges over 100,000 miles for the same transatlantic business class route and layers on fuel surcharges. United MileagePlus charges 70,000–88,000 miles for the same seat. Avianca LifeMiles charges 63,000 miles with zero carrier surcharges. Same seat. Same plane. Wildly different cost.

Avianca keeps rates competitive because they want their program to be attractive to non-Avianca flyers — it's a revenue play. And because their route network is South America-focused, they've built a powerful award program that earns loyalty from customers who may never set foot on an Avianca plane.

Many programs claim no surcharges, then quietly pass through "carrier-imposed fees" that look indistinguishable from surcharges. LifeMiles is one of the genuine exceptions. On partner award bookings — including Lufthansa, Swiss, and other carriers that traditionally levy heavy surcharges — LifeMiles charges only government taxes. For a JFK–FRA business class award, expect to pay roughly $50–$150 out of pocket. That's the full cash outlay.

This is where the transfer partner ecosystem matters. LifeMiles accepts transfers from:

The instant Citi transfer is particularly powerful: if you find available award space today, you can move points and call LifeMiles to book within the same session. Capital One and Bilt are nearly as fast. Marriott's 3:1 ratio makes it less efficient unless you have a large Bonvoy balance and no better option.

LifeMiles runs frequent purchased miles sales, often 100%+ bonus miles on purchases. This is a legitimate strategy for topping off your balance when you're a few thousand miles short of a redemption. Combined with transfer partners, it creates significant flexibility. Watch for promotions at lifemiles.com — they typically appear 6–8 times per year.

The golden rule of any points transfer: never transfer miles until you've confirmed award availability. LifeMiles miles are non-refundable once transferred, and award space can disappear in hours.

United MileagePlus has one of the best Star Alliance partner award search tools available to the public. Go to united.com, start a search as if you're booking an award ticket, and look for business class availability on Lufthansa or Swiss flights on your target route. United displays Lufthansa partner space accurately in most cases. You're looking for "saver" level availability — marked as "X" class on Lufthansa.

Lufthansa's own website (lufthansa.com) sometimes shows availability that United misses, and vice versa. Search both. You're not booking here — just confirming the seat exists.

An ExpertFlyer subscription ($10/month) lets you set availability alerts for specific routes and dates. For a high-value redemption like this, it's often worth one month of the service to monitor your target window.

LifeMiles opens its booking window 355 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer transatlantic, major European events — set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Business class award space on Lufthansa releases in small batches and fills quickly.

Once you've confirmed space, act fast. Log into your points program and initiate the transfer:

Transfer exactly what you need — 63,000 miles for a one-way business class transatlantic award — plus a small buffer of 2,000–3,000 miles for potential routing variations.

Go to lifemiles.com and search your award. The website has improved but can still be inconsistent with partner availability display. If the online search doesn't show the space you found on United.com, call LifeMiles directly at their customer service line. Have your flight numbers, dates, and cabin class ready. Phone agents can access and book partner availability that the website sometimes fails to display.

After booking, you'll receive a confirmation email with a PNR (record locator). Verify this on the operating carrier's website — go to lufthansa.com or swiss.com and look up your reservation using the PNR. If it pulls up correctly, your booking is solid. Save this confirmation and check it once more 72 hours before departure.

Avianca LifeMiles uses a distance-based award chart for Star Alliance partner flights, and their chart is consistently 15-40% cheaper than competing programs for the same seats. The reason is strategic: Avianca wants to attract members to its loyalty program, and aggressive pricing on aspirational redemptions is how they compete with larger alliances. For you, this means the exact same Lufthansa First Class seat or ANA business class seat costs significantly fewer points when booked through LifeMiles versus through United MileagePlus or the carrier directly. The catch is that LifeMiles availability depends on the operating carrier releasing award space to partners, so you still need to search on the carrier or United.com before transferring.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's walk through a real redemption so you can see exactly what this looks like in practice.

The Route: New York JFK → Frankfurt FRA, nonstop The Aircraft: Lufthansa Boeing 747-8, upper deck business class The Cash Price: $6,500 (a realistic peak-season transatlantic business class fare) The Points Cost: 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles Out-of-Pocket Fees: ~$85 in government taxes CPP Achieved: 10.3 cents per point

You've transferred 63,000 Citi ThankYou points to LifeMiles — instantly — spotted the award space on United.com the morning it opened, called LifeMiles to confirm, and had your booking locked in within 90 minutes of finding the seat.

Lufthansa's 747-8 upper deck business class is one of the most iconic products in commercial aviation. The upper deck seats — in a 2-2-2 configuration — sit quieter and smoother than the main deck, with fewer passengers and a more intimate cabin feel.

Your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet. You'll have direct aisle access (depending on your seat selection), a large personal entertainment screen, and Lufthansa's catering, which consistently ranks among the top transatlantic carriers. The meal service on JFK–FRA is legitimate: a proper multi-course dinner, a breakfast service as you approach Germany, and a snack menu available throughout.

Before you board, you'll have access to Lufthansa's business class lounge at JFK — typically the Lufthansa Business Lounge or, depending on timing, the partner lounge. Hot food, showers, and a genuine departure experience that costs nothing beyond the taxes you've already paid.

The flight itself is roughly 7.5 hours. In a flat bed, that's a real night's sleep — or close enough. You arrive in Frankfurt rested, which matters whether you're connecting onward or starting your trip immediately.

For the ChooseFI community: this is the redemption that pays for the honeymoon, the milestone anniversary trip, or the family adventure you've been planning since you first discovered travel rewards. The $6,500 you didn't spend stays in your index funds.

Book at the 355-day mark for peak dates. Lufthansa releases a small number of partner award seats when the schedule opens. The travelers who get summer business class awards are almost always the ones who searched on day 355. Set a calendar alert. Be ready.

Use Citi ThankYou for time-sensitive bookings. Because Citi transfers to LifeMiles are instant, you can find award space and complete your booking in a single session. This matters when you're racing to secure a specific seat before someone else grabs it.

Watch for LifeMiles purchased miles promotions. If you're 10,000–15,000 miles short of a redemption, purchasing miles during a 100% bonus promotion can effectively cost you 0.5–0.7 cents per mile — still leaving you with excellent overall CPP on the redemption. Check lifemiles.com regularly or set a Google Alert for "LifeMiles promotion."

Verify your booking on the operating carrier's website. After booking through LifeMiles, always look up your PNR on lufthansa.com or swiss.com. If it appears correctly, your seat is real. If it doesn't, call LifeMiles immediately.

Search Swiss as an alternative to Lufthansa. Swiss International Air Lines is also a Star Alliance member, also bookable through LifeMiles at the same rates, and also operates excellent business class products on transatlantic routes. Swiss often has more partner award availability than Lufthansa on certain dates.

Never transfer points before confirming availability. This is the most common — and most expensive — mistake in travel rewards. LifeMiles does not allow re-transfers out of the program.

Don't ignore the miles expiry policy. LifeMiles expire 12 months from your last earning activity. Any account activity — earning miles, purchasing miles, even a credit card transaction — resets the clock on your entire balance. Set a recurring reminder every 10 months to run a small transaction if you're holding a balance without an imminent booking.

Don't book Lufthansa First Class expecting the same experience. Lufthansa's First Class is a separate product with separate availability and pricing. Business class is the sweet spot here — outstanding value, more seats, and significantly better availability.

Avoid mixing Marriott Bonvoy transfers with tight timelines. At 3:1 and 1–5 days transfer time, Bonvoy is the slowest and least efficient path into LifeMiles. Plan accordingly.

This redemption is built for the experienced FI traveler who has already earned their first free night or domestic flight and is ready to graduate to aspirational international business class. You don't need to fly business class constantly — but for a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or a long-planned European trip, this is the redemption that makes the experience extraordinary without derailing your savings rate.

You need 63,000 LifeMiles per person, per direction. A couple flying one-way needs 126,000 miles. Most people will get there through a combination of one or two travel credit card welcome bonuses and organic spending — entirely achievable within the FI community's existing card strategy.

## Rated: Hard — Here's Why This redemption earns its **hard** rating from three compounding challenges, none of which is insurmountable but all of which require deliberate effort. **Challenge 1: Award Availability Is Limited.** Lufthansa releases partner award seats conservatively. You may search for weeks before finding space on your preferred route and dates. This isn't a redemption where you decide Tuesday you want to go and book Thursday. You need a booking window of weeks to months, and flexibility in your travel dates helps enormously. **Challenge 2: The Booking Process Has Friction.** LifeMiles' website doesn't always surface partner award availability accurately. You'll likely need to search on United.com to find the space, then call LifeMiles to actually book it. That phone call requires patience — hold times vary, and you'll need to clearly communicate flight numbers, dates, and cabin class to the agent. **Challenge 3: Timing the Transfer Is High-Stakes.** Because you can't transfer points *out* of LifeMiles, you're committing your points the moment you initiate a transfer. Finding the seat, moving the miles, and completing the booking requires confidence and speed. ## How to Overcome the Challenges 1. **Start searching early** — 300+ days out for peak travel. Use ExpertFlyer alerts to monitor availability passively. 2. **Use Citi ThankYou for instant transfers** so you can act immediately when you find a seat. 3. **Practice the phone booking process** once before your high-stakes redemption — call LifeMiles with a simple question to understand their system. If you've successfully booked one or two simpler awards before, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has members completing this redemption every year — and every single one says the boarding moment made the effort completely worth it.

United shows Star Alliance partner availability that LifeMiles can book. Search for Saver-level awards in business or first class on your target route. Note the exact carrier, flight number, and date.

Log into LifeMiles.com and run the same search. Confirm the flight appears and note the exact mileage required. Some partner space visible on United may not be available through LifeMiles, so always double-check.

Amex MR, Chase UR, Citi ThankYou, and Capital One miles all transfer to LifeMiles. Amex transfers are often fastest (same day). Transfer only after confirming availability in Step 2.

Premium cabin award space is limited and competitive. Once your transferred miles appear in your LifeMiles account, complete the booking immediately. Do not wait — the seat can be taken by another searcher.

LifeMiles charges low taxes and fees on most partner awards, typically $30-$100 depending on the route. Some carriers (notably British Airways) add fuel surcharges, but most Star Alliance carriers keep fees minimal through LifeMiles.

Yes, Lufthansa First Class is bookable through LifeMiles at 87,000 miles one-way from the US to Europe. Availability is limited and typically released at 14 days before departure for partner programs, though some space appears further out. Search on United.com first to confirm Lufthansa First saver space exists before transferring.

Transfer times vary by partner. Amex Membership Rewards transfers often post same-day. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers typically take 1-2 business days. Citi ThankYou and Capital One transfers can take 1-3 days. Always account for transfer time when booking time-sensitive award space.

Most Star Alliance carriers booked through LifeMiles have low or no fuel surcharges. The notable exception is British Airways (a oneworld carrier, not bookable through LifeMiles). Taxes and fees on typical Star Alliance routes run $30-$100 per ticket, making LifeMiles one of the cheapest programs for out-of-pocket award costs.

If the booking fails because award space disappeared between your search and transfer, the miles sit in your LifeMiles account. They do not expire as long as you have account activity every 12 months. You can use them for a future booking, but you cannot transfer them back to your original program.

Avianca LifeMiles is the program that lets FI-community travelers fly the same premium cabins as frequent business travelers at a fraction of the points cost. By consistently underpricing Star Alliance awards, LifeMiles turns 63,000-87,000 transferable points into experiences worth $8,000 or more. The process requires discipline (never transfer before confirming availability), patience (searching for saver space takes time), and a willingness to navigate a less polished booking experience. But the value is real: 15-20 cents per point on aspirational flights that would be unreachable at cash prices.

#8613. Investing $10,000 – Fill a Roth IRA, Then Buy a Broad Index Fund

For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. With $10,000 to invest, use accounts with tax breaks before a regular one. Take any 401(k) match you’re missing, pay off high-interest debt, and top up your emergency fund. Then fill this year’s Roth IRA, and put the rest in a broad, low-cost index fund in a brokerage account.

The account you choose matters more than the fund you buy.

Accounts with tax breaks have yearly limits you can’t make up later, while a brokerage account takes any amount, any time. Work down this list until the money runs out.

Say you get the match, owe nothing on cards, and have a full emergency fund. If you’re under 50, this year’s limit, $7,500, goes in the Roth and the rest in a total-market index fund.

Invest it all at once, since Vanguard’s research found a lump sum beat splitting it into three monthly purchases about two-thirds of the time from 1976 to 2022. If a drop right after would rattle you, dollar-cost averaging, spreading it over a few months, is fine too.

Skip hot stocks, and don’t pay an advisor 1% a year to manage it. At an assumed 7% yearly return, that fee leaves you 6%, so $10,000 grows to about $57,400 in 30 years instead of $76,100.

Buy the index fund the day each deposit arrives, since the money sits in cash until you choose an investment.

#8612. Giant Crabs Complicate New Amelia Earhart Search

Researchers hunting for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s plane have followed new clues to a remote Pacific atoll, inhabited by giant coconut crabs so large and active at night that the team sleeps aboard its ship for safety.

In 1932, the American aviation pioneer became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. Five years later, she and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared while attempting to circumnavigate the globe. After leaving Papua New Guinea on July 2, they failed to reach Howland Island, their planned refueling stop. The official account is that navigation and communication problems caused their Lockheed Electra to run out of fuel and crash into the ocean. The disappearance has produced decades of speculation about what happened.

Amelia Earhart beside her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. 1937. Photo: National Portrait Gallery

One long-standing hypothesis, advanced mainly by the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, is that the pair reached Nikumaroro (then known as Gardner Island), about 350 nautical miles southeast of Howland, landed on the reef, and later died as castaways.

A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University arrived at the uninhabited atoll — part of Kiribati — this week after a 1,500km voyage on their vessel, according to the BBC and Purdue University updates. They are investigating the Taraia Object, an elongated shape in a lagoon first identified in satellite imagery in 2020 and visible in aerial photos dating to 1938.

Some researchers view it as a possible remnant of Earhart’s plane. Others consider it more likely a fallen tree or other debris. This marks the first authorized visit to the island in seven years, and the first to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15 years.

The uninhabited Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean. Photo: Wikipedia

The work, which should take about five days, includes clearing vegetation, scanning for metal, and using dredging equipment to examine the object, which lies only about three meters from shore in as little as 1.5m of water, depending on the tides. Conditions have already limited boat access on some days, though organizers expect an update on the object’s identity within about 48 hours, according to Purdue.

The coconut crab has the strongest pinch of any crustacean. Photo: Reinhard Dirscherl via treehugger.com

The island’s coconut crabs, also called robber crabs, are the world’s largest land-dwelling invertebrates, with a leg span of up to one meter and a body weight of more than four kilos. They can lift objects weighing about 28kg, crack open coconuts, climb trees, and emerge at night to capture live prey such as rats and seabirds, as well as carrion. Expedition communications stated that the crabs’ size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical, so the crew returns to the ship each night.

The same animals appear in theories about what might have happened if Earhart died on Nikumaroro. In 1940, British colonists recovered 13 bones near the remains of a fire. The bones were later lost, though some re-analyses of the recorded measurements have suggested consistency with a woman of Earhart’s stature.

The Taraia Object on a satellite image. Photo: Rick Pettigrew/Archaeological Legacy Institute

In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery placed pig carcasses on a similar island and found that coconut crabs (along with smaller hermit crabs) stripped most of the flesh and dragged bones to burrows in less than two weeks. The crabs are not known to hunt humans aggressively. The primary risk is a powerful defensive pinch from their claws if they are handled or startled.

The survey of the Taraia Object began on Wednesday. The crew established a base camp, cleared overgrown paths, and prepared for their fieldwork.

Previous searches, including one by well-known explorer Robert Ballard, who first located the Titanic, have not produced any aircraft wreckage, and many experts continue to regard an ocean crash near Howland as the most likely outcome. The current team reports encountering some crabs during initial setup but described them as posing no threat to operations at that stage.

The Taraia Object’s survey has begun. Photo: Purdue.edu

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

Home » Make Money » How to Make Money Without a Job: 26 Ways to Earn Money Outside the 9-5

Breaking free from the traditional 9-5 is more achievable than ever with these 26 innovative income streams. Ready to redefine your concept of earning?

Are you trying to win the Mega Millions, but your numbers never seem to come up? It may be time to look for better ways to make money. Fortunately, you can earn extra cash without going and getting a “real job.”

What are the best ways to avoid sitting in a cubicle all day? Some money-making strategies require an upfront investment, while others let you earn money in your free time with the help of apps.

Read on to learn the best ways to earn cash without a regular 9-5 job, plus tips on how almost anyone can get started.

One of the easiest ways to earn money is by signing up to participate in market research studies. You won’t make much, a few dollars here and there, but you can create a free account and get started within minutes.

You’ll be paid in PayPal cash or gift cards for sharing your opinion and completing other tasks online.

E-Poll Market Research is one of the top companies to consider for this type of work. They make it easy to create an account and answer survey questions.

However, there are plenty of other options to consider, including:

While market research gigs won’t make you rich, it’s something you can do during your spare time.

If you have a book idea, turning your story into an eBook can help you earn passive income without a regular job. Kindle Direct Publishing can even help you format your book for Kindle, at which point you can market and sell your book to millions of potential readers who shop on Amazon.com.

How much can you earn writing eBooks? That depends on how many books you write, how much you sell them for, and how successful you are at marketing your book. Selling 20 books per month with a profit of $7 per book would net you $140 per month and $1,680 per year.

Meanwhile, selling 100 books per month at $7 per book would net you $700 per month and $8,400 per year. Need a little inspiration? Here’s an article that shows you how to make your first $1,000 selling eBooks.

You can earn a lot of money by starting a blog or niche website and monetizing it. I should know. I started Good Financial Cents more than a decade ago, and have earned millions of dollars through the monetization of this site since its earliest days.

How do you make money blogging? Earning real income with a website isn’t as easy as it looks, but there are plenty of monetization strategies you can try.

Here are the most common ways blogs make money:

If you’re curious about what it takes to earn money blogging, consider signing up for my Make 1K Challenge. It’s free and can help you earn your first $1,000 online with some of the blog monetization strategies I’ve already mentioned.

You could argue that freelance work is like a regular job, but working at home and on your terms is much different from traditional employment. The fact is, most freelancers are fully remote – they can work from anywhere in the world with a laptop and an internet connection.

Plus, they can hire and fire clients based on their personal needs and preferences, and their income potential is unlimited. According to ZipRecruiter, freelancers in the U.S. average $63.53 per hour.

Of course, you’ll need a marketable skill to find paid work as a freelancer. This could be freelance writing, design skills, marketing expertise, or something else.

You can use several websites to market your skills as a freelancer, including:

HealthyWage makes it possible to earn money while you lose weight. You won’t earn a ton of cash through the app, but you can earn a few dollars and use it to supplement other income you have.

The more weight you lose, the more money you can make. For example, the HealthyWage website claims some of their clients who lost more than 100 pounds managed to earn anywhere from $1,400 to $3,000.

However, the HW weight loss calculator shows potential earnings of $578 to $828 for people who only have 15 pounds to lose.

If you have a car you rarely use and want to earn some side income, you can consider renting it out with Turo, a ride-sharing platform that connects car owners with people who need a short-term rental. You can set your price, although you’ll have more success if you price your car competitively.

Nicer vehicles in high-demand areas can easily fetch rates that surpass $100 per day through this platform. Turo notes that in-demand cars rented out regularly can bring in anywhere from $10,000 to $20,000 per year in net profit.

Plus, almost anyone can rent out their car provided it meets the guidelines of the Turo platform. Your car must be 12 years old or newer with less than 130,000 miles. It must be worth less than $200,000 (no Lambo’s), and you must also meet Turo’s auto insurance requirements.

Do you have a spare bedroom in your home that you never use? Maybe you have a basement or garage apartment you could fix up and begin renting for a profit?

Either way, Airbnb lets you rent out rooms and other spaces in your home on any dates you prefer. You must let renters know they’re renting a room in a home vs. an entire apartment or house and provide as much additional detail as possible.

The amount you can earn will depend on where you live and the type of accommodation you can offer. However, expensive cities like Chicago, New York, and San Francisco have plenty of rooms for rent that go for well over $100 per night.

You may not have an entire room you can rent, but even if you have some storage space, Neighbor.com allows you to rent it out to others in need.

Common spaces rented through this platform include

The Neighbor.com platform makes it easy to advertise your unused space so that people nearby can inquire if they’re interested. Also, note that the platform offers insurance that can protect you if some of your client’s items are damaged or stolen while in your care.

How much can you make renting out extra space? It depends on how much space you have to rent and where it’s located. However, Neighbor.com shows a range of rental space options that cost anywhere from $20 to $100+ per month.

Investing in dividend stocks is one of the best ways to earn money without a regular job. Many early retirees find a way to live and pay bills based solely on the dividends they receive from various stocks.

But what exactly is a dividend stock? For the most part, they are regular stocks but with a track record of sharing their profits with investors through dividends.

Dividends can also be earned in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds, and they can be significant once you build up a large portfolio.

Since dividends are paid by profitable companies, they tend to be seen as less risky for investors. If you’re curious about what it takes to get started with this strategy, this post explains how to invest in dividend stocks.

Housesitting is an option if you’re somewhat mobile and can move from place to place. Generally, you can find house-sitting gigs through word of mouth, referrals, or online portals like Craigslist.org or Facebook Marketplace.

That said, not all house-sitting gigs are paid. Some offer the potential for exotic travel instead and free lodging for a week to several months.

Either way, a website called TrustedHousesitters is the best place to find house-sitting gigs. Some jobs posted are for house-sitting only, while others require house sitters to provide basic care for pets or plants.

If you have serious wanderlust and want to travel far and wide, this platform can help make it happen. Many gigs posted online are in countries like Australia, Ireland, France, and Switzerland.

If you love animals and want to earn money taking care of them, several platforms can help turn your dream into a reality.

For example, Rover.com lets you provide basic care for dogs or cats in your home, or you can pick up dog walking gigs. Another mobile app, called Wag!, lets you do more of the same.

You can set your rates for all types of work through these platforms, and your availability. While earnings vary by location and job, most people watch dogs and cats for anywhere from $40 to $100 per night.

Real estate investing may seem like a pipe dream if you hope to earn income without a job but hear me out. There are many ways to earn income through real estate without owning physical property or dealing with the hassles of being a landlord.

You can invest in real estate investment trusts (REITs) that let you build wealth over time. You can also use a platform called Fundrise to invest in real estate with a minimum investment of $10.

Fundrise lets you purchase eREITs, large investment funds that acquire, own, or operate multi-residential and commercial properties. The income you earn is entirely passive since it handles the work of finding income-producing properties and managing them.

While returns are never guaranteed, Fundrise investors have achieved very solid returns. Investors who use the platform earned an average return of 7.31% in 2020, followed by 22.99% in 2021, 1.50% in 2022 and -7.45% in 2023 (their first down year).

You can earn income on your spare change by investing it using Acorns. The roundup savings app syncs to your debit or credit card rounds up every purchase you make to the nearest dollar, and invests the difference. Once it’s set up, there’s no work on your part.

Most of the money is invested in ETFs and managed by the world’s top investment firms like Vanguard and BlackRock. While this app makes it easy to invest small amounts of money, it’s not free to use. Personal plans start at $3 per month, while a family plan costs just $5.

If you’re looking for some paid gigs that are relatively easy, consider setting up a profile on TaskRabbit, an online platform that lets you get paid for completing various tasks, such as:

Projects typically pay between $30 and $100, although some pay significantly more than that. TaskRabbit also lets you pick and choose the jobs you want to take on based on your availability so that you can work entirely on your schedule.

If you love taking photographs and have a knack for getting professional-looking images, you can use your skills and expertise to sell photos online.

Websites like Depositphotos and iStockPhoto pay photographers to supply them with stock photos they can sell to writers, publications, and various online platforms.

The best part about this side hustle is that you can get started with the equipment you already have. While you can use a professional camera if you want to, many smartphones take professional-quality photos.

Earning a bank bonus is another way to earn money without a regular job, but you’ll need an upfront investment to get started. Most bonus offers require you to deposit a specific amount of money and keep it in your account for up to 12 months.

You may also be required to set up direct deposit to earn a bank bonus, and other terms and conditions may apply.

Where can you find the best bank bonuses? While bonus offers constantly change, you can start by checking with banks like Chase, HSBC, Radius Bank, and Wells Fargo.

Flipping furniture requires some upfront legwork and potentially even some artistic talent, but you can earn a solid income with this strategy if you know what you’re doing.

Essentially, this side hustle requires you to shop at thrift stores, garage sales, and online platforms to find furniture that will ultimately sell for more than you paid.

From there, you can sell the furniture as-is or clean it up and paint it with the goal of fetching an even higher price.

You can make money driving for Uber or Lyft on your own time, picking and choosing the days and hours you want to work.

Not only is rideshare work one of the most flexible side hustles, but you can earn $20 per hour and more with tips.

If you are low on free time but still want to make money without a job, consider selling stuff you don’t need. An array of online platforms makes it a breeze, although some platforms work better for selling.

For example, you can use Poshmark to earn money selling used clothing and accessories, while used electronics tend to sell best on platforms like eBay.com, Decluttr, BuyBackWorld, and Gazelle.

If you have home decor, furniture, or workout equipment to sell, you’ll almost always do better unloading those items locally on Facebook Marketplace.

Starting a YouTube channel is another way to earn money without a job, but that doesn’t mean it’s not work. The fact is, that creating quality videos and building an audience takes a lot of creativity and time. Plus, not everyone who tries to build a YouTube channel will succeed.

That said, you can earn income without a regular job. I know because I have done it with my YouTube channel, Wealth Hacker.

How much you can earn on YouTube varies quite a bit, but it’s possible to earn thousands of dollars per month. If you’re curious about monetizing videos, my in-depth guide will show you how to make money on YouTube.

Donating plasma is a unique way to earn money without a job, although it’s not very glamorous. DonatingPlasma.org makes it easy to find plasma donation centers in your area, and you can earn as much as $100 for your first donation.

That said, subsequent plasma donations typically earn closer to $50. You’ll also be limited by the number of times you can donate plasma within a month. However, it’s possible to use this side gig to earn an extra $500 per month, which you can use to supplement your primary income.

If you are willing to complete various tasks that help regular workers do their jobs, consider becoming a crowd worker. This gig will have you finishing up to-do lists of jobs that don’t require specific technical skills.

For example, you may get paid to proofread documents, label images, update a resume, complete a form, or complete a data entry assignment.

Several platforms help you find crowd-working gigs, but the best ones include Microworkers and Clickworker.

If you want to do something simple that will get you moving, consider delivering groceries using apps like Instacart or Shipt. You get paid hourly, plus tips and all you have to do is head to the store, purchase groceries according to a list, and deliver them to people in your neighborhood.

The gig is extremely flexible, similar to driving for Uber or Lyft.

Another non-job gig lets you get paid to deliver packages for Amazon.com. You can do this through a platform called Amazon Flex, which promises its drivers anywhere from $18 to $25 per hour.

Unlike a regular Amazon job, Flex lets you pick the day and the hours you want to work. To get started, you need to create a free account, get approved, and start reserving blocks of time you want to deliver packages.

Finally, you can earn money by selling unwanted or unused gift cards in your possession. This hustle is made easy thanks to platforms like GiftDeals.com and CardCash.com.

You won’t get the total value of your gift cards, but you should get 90% or more of the gift card balance for each card you sell. While selling gift cards for less than their total value may not seem ideal, it’s better than not using them and getting nothing in return.

Finally, you can earn small amounts of money by signing up with the best online survey sites. Not only is this side hustle as easy as it gets, but you can participate and get paid during your spare time and even on your phone.

Other online survey sites to check out include the following:

With all this being said, you’ll want to keep in mind that most surveys only pay a few bucks and that some only pay you with gift cards, while others offer the option for PayPal transfers. Make sure you understand how each survey site works and how you get paid before you sign up.

There you have it, 26 ways to make money without a job. While many of the jobs on our list won’t replace your 9-5, they can be a great way to increase your income so you can pay off debt or break the cycle of living paycheck to paycheck.

Check out the video below if you’re looking for even more ways to make money.
