#8609. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re currently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country.  They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.)

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some new models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

But in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

So right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re quickly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Great question – I tried to cover this in the article under the heading, “Why haven’t I noticed prices going up yet?”

First of all, most of the tariffs (or threatened tariffs) haven’t even hit yet.

But even when they do, the end result will be a bit unpredictable. Importers can of course shift supply to countries with lower tariffs or even domestic suppliers. Consumers will also react to rising prices by scaling back their spending, which shifts prices back down the supply/demand curve a little.

In the extreme case, high tariffs can even cause a recession which lowers demand for almost all goods and services, which means that prices for domestically produced services with elastic pricing might go down and bring the overall inflation numbers back in check. In other words, some people lose their jobs so on average there’s less money being spent on restaurants -> restaurants have to lower their prices.

Heck, in a good enough recession even house prices and rents will drop, which is the biggest factor in the inflation basket.

Might be semantic, but maybe tariffs are not “inflation”. It would be like saying that a VAT would be inflationary. Instead, this is a one-time step-function change in the cost of goods, then inflation (velocity) resumes on the new cost base. Oren Cass had an interesting blog article on this last week. At least food for thought – he posits that economists don’t actually think tariffs are inflationary.

100% the case. Inflation is caused by an increase in the money supply, by definition. It means your purchasing power is worth less. A one-time increase in a specific category of goods of 15% is not “inflation.” Meanwhile, every time the government uses printed (or digitally entered) dollars to spend trillions they don’t have, inflation grows massively and compounds, and for some reason, the majority of people don’t bat an eye.

A great analogy for inflation would be something like this… You are in charge of the county fair. There are a bunch of vendors of popcorn, cotton candy, and ride like ferris wheels, etc. You print tickets that visitors can use to acquire these goods and ride these rides, and the vendors set their own ticket prices. You and your friends discover you can give yourselves tickets and get more popcorn and ride more rides since you own the ticket machine. With the flood of tickets, the vendors realize they can (and need to) raise their prices. This is inflation. And it doesn’t matter if it’s due to your and your friends doing it for yourselves, or just doing it because of more guests coming to the fair (for “growth”).

I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply. Money supply is one factor in that, but so is the overall supply and demand of everything that is for sale. Money supply is increased or decreased as needed in reaction to what’s happening with prices, in order to keep prices more stable, if the system is well managed.

In your county fair example, you are holding the number of vendors and the items and quantities for sale as a constant while increasing the number of tickets. In reality the fair’s mini-economy will grow and shrink over time, and if the ticket supply were forced to always stay constant the ticket prices of rides, popcorn and cotton candy would move up and down significantly in reaction.

“I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply.”

But the employment report shows it as a net positive.

I believe that this effect does two things:

Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

2000 US Debt ($5.7 trillion) Source: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/historical-debt-outstanding/historical-debt-outstanding

Current US Debt ($36.2 trillion Source: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/historical-debt-outstanding/historical-debt-outstanding

2016 Nominal US GDP Growth (3.2%) Source: https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/34c0c783-f785-459c-a93a-2997c6abb8b4/01-30-gdp-review.pdf

2019 Nominal US GDP Growth (4.1%) Source: https://www.bea.gov/news/2020/gross-domestic-product-fourth-quarter-and-year-2019-advance-estimate#:~:text=Current%2Ddollar%20GDP%20increased%204.1,table%201%20and%20table%203).

US Federal deficit as percentage of GDP Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYFSGDA188S

Also, I think it’s worth flagging the US debt as a proportion of GDP, which is the key statistic vs. just thinking of the absolute figure. There are different ways to slice the US debt, but they all tell the same story. Just taking the basic total US debt relative to GDP shows a rise from 54% at year ending 2000 to 121% as of 1Q2025. That is staggeringly scary. Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GFDEGDQ188S

Another after thought, while nominal GDP matters for the annual deficit, that is not to say real GDP doesn’t matter in a silo. They both have relevance. Clearly the US government has more control over expenses, and to a somewhat lesser extent revenue, than it does inflation. For 2024, the deficit ran at 6.28% of GDP. If inflation, which most of us can agree above a low percentage is typically bad, drops back into a ~2% range but real GDP growth runs in the 2-3% range, which is decent growth, then we’re still only growing nominal GDP at 4-5% vs. 6%+ under the state-of-play. Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYFSGDA188S) Source: https://www.bea.gov/news/2025/gross-domestic-product-4th-quarter-and-year-2024-second-estimate

This is an interesting analysis. The way I summed it up to an acquaintance is that Trump is playing with fire. In the end, it may be that we have something nice and shiny as a result. However, it is just as likely (if not more) that this whole thing is a dumpster fire and in the end it will just a smoking heap of ash.

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

#8608. Image of Elephant Carrying Dead Calf Wins Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026

Federico Veronesi was following a family of elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he came upon a strange and tragic sight. A female elephant was carrying the stiff body of a deceased calf. The Italian wildlife photographer’s shocking image has become the Grand Title Winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Earlier, we reviewed the runner-up entries for this year, released back in September. One of those entries included Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen’s photo of an orca carrying a deceased calf, which it repeatedly lifted up out of the water. These striking images of animals mourning speak to the contest’s mission. Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum, says it strives to “demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently.”

Other category winners explore the relationship between the wild and urban worlds, document natural beauty, and capture more playful wildlife moments.

Winner of the Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category, Alex Visbal’s image shows how artificially dividing a Utah wetland has cut part of it off from freshwater, resulting in pink-producing, high-salinity microbes. Photo: Alex Visbal/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

While images like Visbal and Veronesi’s capture large scenes and massive animals, other winners focus on tiny, hidden natural worlds. Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas of Germany won the Rising Star Portfolio Award for his series exploring the smallest and least noticed animals.

As not all of our readers are as fond of arachnids as I am, we feature Tinker-Tsavalas’ whimsical image of a teensy springtail exploring moss, rather than his portraits of ground crab spiders or harvestmen. Photo: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Below even the insect level are the works of macro photographer Kutub Uddin. He won the Portfolio Award for his series of surreal slime mold landscapes. Like Tinker-Tsavalas, Uddin uses focus stacking to achieve incredible fine detail.

This fruiting slime mold looks like some sort of whimsical, slightly grotesque bonsai. Photo: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Several winners focused on wildlife in non-wild settings. Loren Elliott won the Photojournalist Story Award for his series following the coyotes of San Francisco. There are around 100 coyotes living in and around San Francisco, and their relationship with human residents is close, but fraught.

There were several excellent shots in this series, but I would be failing you if I didn’t highlight this one. These two coyote pups live in a den on a golf course, leaving them plenty of golf balls to play with. Photo: Loren Elliott/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Across the world in Bangkok, common water monitors have also become city dwellers. Seth Forestson won in the Urban Wildlife category for his image of a lizard triumphantly bearing a fish through a public park. In the background, the city skyline rises in dramatic contrast.

Photo: Seth Forestson/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Meanwhile, the Plants and Fungi category winner comes from the weird world of mushrooms. On Mount Olympus, Agorastos Papatsanis used ultraviolet light to reveal the luminescence of Mycena renati. Commonly known as beautiful bonnet, the stems of these mushrooms glow a neon yellow.

Photo: Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

The Young Grand Title Winner, who entered in the 11-14 year-old category, is Oscar Whitfield. In Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park, Whitfield captured the efforts of a dung beetle.

Ancient Egyptian cosmology drew parallels between the scarab beetle, pushing a ball of dung, and Khepri, the scarab-headed deity, pushing the sun across the sky. The dung beetle also plays a vital role environmentally. The way they process and bury dung reduces methane production and helps speed decomposition. Photo: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

You can view the full gallery on the Natural History Museum website. Tickets to the full exhibition in London, England are available here.

The full view of Federico Veronesi’s contest-winning image. Photo: Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8607. Summits Begin on Ama Dablam, Late Fall's Most Popular Peak

With the failure of commercial climbs on Manaslu and Dhaulagiri this fall, all eyes now turn to the most popular commercial peak in the second half of autumn — 6,812m Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team already opened the route to the summit last Tuesday.

Unlike those two 8,000m peaks, where bad conditions prompted outfitters to abort the season prematurely, the seven rope fixers on Ama Dablam experienced light winds, sunshine, and good snow, which allowed them to fix 800m of rope in just five hours. Siddhi Bahadur Tamang, Lal Kumar Tamang, Dawa Paljor Sherpa, Lakpa Sangay Sherpa, Pasang Tenji Sherpa, and Namgel Dorje Tamang stood on top of Ama Dablam on October 13 shortly before noon:

Since then, workers have been hurrying to set up and stock three higher camps, while many climbers flock to Base Camp or acclimatize on nearby peaks before their summit push.

According to the October 13 update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism, 178 permits for foreign climbers have been issued for Ama Dablam. That will increase greatly over the coming weeks, since the high season continues until the end of November. In recent years, improved logistics and increased popularity have led to many more summits. Success rates are also far better than just a few years ago.

Last fall, according to the Himalayan Database (HDB), 273 foreigners attempted to climb — and all succeeded! They were supported by 399 Sherpas, including guides, high-altitude porters, and their helpers. The final summit numbers included the 273 foreigners plus 227 locals, totaling 500 summits, with a 100% summit rate. Two clients died: a Brazilian climber hit by falling ice on his way down, and a South Korean man who suffered cardiac arrest.

By comparison, in 2015, 76 foreigners and 47 locals summited — nearly five times fewer — and the summit rate was 71%. Certain things have not changed: Back then, the normal route was also fixed, and teams had Sherpa support. It’s the scale and the tactics that are different.

Ama Dablam Base Camp. Photo: Dominic Asselin

If Everest is to Himalayan climbing history what Mont Blanc was to the Alps, Ama Dablam is the Nepalese equivalent of the Matterhorn: a favorite of both climbers and outfitters, for different reasons.

Climbers appreciate its beauty — it’s usually considered one of the most aesthetic peaks in the world, despite its commercialization, with ropes, abundant Sherpa support, and helicopter transfers. Moreover, the views of Everest, Lhotse, and the surrounding peaks from its flat, snowy summit are breathtaking:

Its relatively low altitude means shorter acclimatization. Climbers usually do a trekking peak and/or hypoxic training at home as preparation. An Ama Dablam climb rarely requires supplemental oxygen — although it is available if needed.

Its convenient location in the Khumbu Valley on the way to Everest is a great asset, thanks to its many year-round accommodations, good infrastructure, an easy peak to acclimatize for, and a straightforward approach trek.

A crowded camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Lakpa Sherpa/8K Expeditions

For outfitters, Ama Dablam is a natural moneymaker. Its wide Base Camp on a dry, flat plain allows a large number of tents, a helipad, and the constant flow of supplies from the Khumbu’s main trail nearby. Yet the key to accommodating many climbers lies in fast expeditions. Once acclimatized, climbers can summit Ama Dablam and return down in three or four days — even less for the frequent speed climbers. That allows companies to reuse the tents and equipment many times through the season. Camp staff and guides are constantly working, with little downtime.

As for the climb itself, double ropes allow climbers to ascend and descend at the same time, maintaining a steady flow of people every day while the weather holds. Last year, there were 10 to 30 summits a day between October 12 and October 27, and nearly every day in November.

File image of climbers on Ama Dablam, progressing on fixed ropes. Photo: Explore-Share

Even during winter, which in Nepal officially starts on December 1, it is common for some teams to attempt Ama Dablam, especially before the end of the year. Expert winter climbers such as Simone Moro often mention the cold but stable and sunny days in Nepal in December. In recent winter attempts on Manaslu, Moro has acclimatized on Ama Dablam.

Nima Rinji, Simone Moro, and Oswald Pereira acclimatized on Ama Dablam in December 2024 before attempting Manaslu in winter. Photo: Manish Maharjan

Last year, the HDB only registered a three-member expedition that summited the mountain in winter. However, during the 2024-25 cold season, 12 foreign climbers and six Sherpas summited that December.

Ama Dablam was first climbed in March 1961 by Mike Gill and Wally Romanes of New Zealand, Mike Ward of the UK, and Barry Bishop of the U.S. via the Southwest Ridge.

Some local operators keep a functioning Base Camp and maintained route on Ama Dablam throughout December. Photo: Seven Summit Treks

With all this latter-day success and improved logistics, the biggest risk may be underestimating Ama Dablam. A high number of rescues have occurred in the last few years. Helicopters can perform long-line airlifts from Camp 3, but such options are not available in bad weather. The prospect of a rescue helicopter on standby in case of trouble, especially on the way down, may produce a false sense of security for those who find themselves at their limits but still decide to continue to the summit.

While the death rates on Ama Dablam are relatively low, it is not a peak to be trifled with, as the many cases of frostbite, AMS, and injuries from falling rock and ice attest.

A helicopter performs a rescue at Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Nga Tenji Sherpa

#8606. Your First $1,000 – Cushion, Card Debt, Then One Fund in a Roth IRA

For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Send your first $1,000 to the earliest step you haven’t finished: a starter emergency fund, then any credit card balance, then a Roth IRA holding one broad fund. Collect your full 401(k) match from your paycheck along the way. It’s an instant return, and none of it comes out of the $1,000.

Investing the $1,000 first feels like progress. But with no savings, the next surprise bill goes on a credit card, and you pay card interest to keep the $1,000 invested.

Paying off a card earns a guaranteed return equal to its interest rate. On card accounts that were charged interest, that rate averaged 22.36% in August, according to the Federal Reserve. No investment promises that. For other loans, the interest rate decides whether to pay them off before investing.

Then comes the Roth IRA, a retirement account you fund with money you’ve already paid tax on. You can contribute if you have pay from work and your income is under the IRS limit. Its growth comes out tax-free after age 59½, as long as five years have passed since the first tax year you contributed for. What you put in can come back out anytime without tax or penalty, so a first investment there stays within reach.

To find your step, ask whether your starter emergency fund is full and whether you carry a card balance. Whatever the answer, collect any 401(k) match your employer offers, since it comes out of your paycheck, not the $1,000. A 50% match adds 50 cents to every dollar it covers, so raise your contribution now if you aren’t getting all of it.

Say you already get the match, your fund is $600 short, and you owe $400 on a card. Put $600 into savings, pay off the card, and open the Roth IRA with your next paycheck.

In the Roth IRA, buy one fund. Pick a broad index fund that tracks the whole U.S. stock market, or a target-date fund for the year you plan to retire, a mix of stocks and bonds that shifts toward bonds as that year nears. Skip single stocks, so the $1,000 doesn’t depend on one company.

Moving the money into the account doesn’t invest it. It waits as cash until you place the order, so buy the fund as soon as the money arrives.

#8604. Tesla Shows Off Flying Roadster: Don’t Buy the Hype

Note: We don’t often run opinion pieces about products, but we couldn’t resist this commentary from our sister site, GearJunkie, about this week’s demo of Tesla’s flying car.

Tesla has promised a sequel to its original Roadster for nearly a decade. We’ve seen a few different versions over the years, and like much of what CEO Elon Musk promises in his big, flashy presentations, it never really materialized. On Thursday night, the brand debuted a vehicle that it claims will enter production in 2028 with rocket thrusters and a sub-1-second 0-60 time.

I hate to be the one to pee in your Wheaties (figuratively speaking), but if you believe that this car will ever see the road in this form, you’ll believe anything. However, I do have some very valuable NFTs to sell you!

In Short: The Thursday announcement of the second-generation Tesla Roadster showed a lot of unbelievable stuff like a flying rocket car and a car that can hang upside down. You shouldn’t believe any of it.

Largely Lotus, but people loved them. Photo: NetCarShow.com

Largely Lotus, but people loved them. Photo: NetCarShow.com

For a quick history lesson on the Tesla Roadster, it debuted in 2008 and was made through 2012. It was based on a modified Lotus Elise chassis, hit 60mph in as little as 3.7 seconds, and travels 244 miles on a charge (according to the EPA). It was the first production electric vehicle to exceed 200 miles of range.

Then, in 2017, Tesla announced its second-generation Roadster alongside a raft of wild claims, including a sub-2-second 0-60 time and a “SpaceX option package” that would add cold-gas thrusters to improve performance. The company offered potential buyers the chance to put down a $50,000 deposit to be among the first to receive their vehicle when it entered production in 2020.

This design came and went, without hitting production. Photo: Editor928111, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

This design came and went, without hitting production. Photo: Editor928111, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

In July 2020, Musk claimed the vehicle would be built in California and that production would start in 2021. Of course, the global COVID-19 pandemic knocked everyone for a loop, so the delay seemed reasonable. Then that 2021 date turned into 2023, which turned into 2024…then 2025, and then the company promised a production version would debut in April 2026.

It’s now mid-October, and the production date is 2028, supposedly. See where I’m going with this?

Yeah, that says $5,000 due today with $245,000 due in 10 days for the Thrust version. Photo: Tesla

Yeah, that says $5,000 due today with $245,000 due in 10 days for the Thrust version. Photo: Tesla

The Roadster isn’t the only Tesla vehicle to get these kinds of big promises and keep getting delayed. It happened with the Model 3 and Y, the Cybertruck, and it happened big time with the Semi. For all of these models, Tesla collected paid reservations by the boatload, effectively getting an interest-free loan to keep going while it figured things out. The delays aren’t a fluke; it’s just how Tesla does business.

Through that lens, Tesla’s continued request for a $50,000 deposit on standard Roadsters and $250,000 for “Thrust” models doesn’t look great. The stock market seems to share our skepticism, too: Tesla’s stock price took a nosedive after the dog-and-pony show, dropping about $20 per share.

That downforce number works out to just over 10,200 pounds. Photo: Tesla

That downforce number works out to just over 10,200 pounds. Photo: Tesla

Of course, the 2028 production date isn’t even remotely the wildest claim Musk and his cronies made about this new Roadster. That honor goes to the ground-effect fans and cold-gas thrusters that let the demo vehicle hang upside down and bunny-hop over a row of other Tesla vehicles.

The first problem is that these kinds of thrusters are unlikely to be legal for road use anywhere on Earth with actual laws. Tesla has previously claimed that the thrusters would use compressed air at a working pressure of 10,000 psi. A tank at that pressure would create an almost mind-bogglingly dangerous crash-safety risk, and the risk to other vehicles and pedestrians from 10,000 psi of air exiting the thruster nozzles is also very real. A rapid pressure increase of just 14.5 psi can, for example, rupture a human eardrum.

Using fans to suck a car down to the road isn’t new. The idea dates back to the 1960s and the Chaparral 2J CanAm race car; Brabham tried it in Formula 1 in 1978 with its BT46, and the Gordon Murray Automotive T50 hypercar currently uses a similar system to boost performance. It’s proven tech. Of course, creating the kind of downforce Tesla is talking about, where a car can hang upside down, is a different story. That much downforce would overload any normal road-going suspension, bottoming it out and making it useless, and if the car had a suspension that could handle those loads, it’d be so stiff that, again, it’d be useless.

That sure looks like a stunt car to us. Photo: Tesla

That sure looks like a stunt car to us. Photo: Tesla

Next, this new Roadster looks a lot like a half-assed, reskinned Lamborghini with McLaren-style door hinges. In typical Tesla bread-and-circuses marketing, nobody got a look at any of the technical components, and neither Musk nor Franz von Holzhausen nor Lars Moravy gave any details as to specs or technical aspects. Musk just rambled about sucking the chrome off a trailer hitch and his friend (and arguably one of the worst people in the world), Peter Thiel.

Having a car-shaped object that does specific things very well to be visually appealing or shocking isn’t new. The movie industry has been doing it for decades, and this demonstration, where nobody was allowed to get near the vehicles, definitely has a whiff of Hollywood stunt car about it -– especially if you pause when the underside of the vehicle is shown and it appears to be a hollow shell fixed to a ladder frame.

What I’m saying is that it’s fine to think a flying, kick-flipping rocket car is a fun visual, but take it with a big fat grain of salt. Remember that this is all coming from a man who brought us all the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and its massive data insecurities, heartless job and program cuts that saved taxpayers very little money, and let us not forget “Big Balls.”

On this Tesla announcement, we urge you to follow the sage advice of Chuck D, Flava Flav, and Terminator X: “Don’t Believe the Hype.”

#8603. Direct Stock Purchase Plans Charge Fees – A $0-Commission Broker Usually Costs Less

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A direct stock purchase plan lets you skip the broker, but it can charge you for each purchase, each dividend reinvested, and each sale. It also buys only at set times. Use a $0-commission brokerage account instead, unless the plan charges nothing to buy and its discount on reinvested dividends will outweigh the sale fee.

A transfer agent such as Computershare, the firm that keeps a company’s shareholder records, runs the plan. Its fees take the biggest bite out of small, regular purchases, like $50 a month into a child’s account or a favorite dividend payer.

Hershey’s plan shows how the fees add up. The first purchase, $250 at minimum, carries no fee. After that, each automatic monthly purchase costs $2.50 plus 5 cents a share, so each $50 purchase loses more than 5% to fees. Reinvesting a dividend costs 5% of it, up to $5, plus 5 cents a share. Selling costs at least $15 plus 12 cents a share, more than 7.5% of a $200 holding.

A brokerage account with $0 commissions and fractional shares, which let $50 buy part of a share, puts the whole $50 into Hershey stock and lets you sell online with no commission. Plans also usually buy and sell at set times, at an average market price, rather than at a price or moment you pick, the SEC notes.

Before you enroll, find the plan’s fee schedule on the company’s investor relations site and check the setup fee and what each purchase, reinvested dividend, and sale costs. A few plans give reinvested dividends a discount on the shares they buy. Omega Healthcare Investors, for one, currently sets a 1% discount on the new shares its plan issues for reinvested dividends. A plan like that beats a $0-commission broker when buying and reinvesting cost nothing and the discount adds up to more than the fee to sell.

For any other stock, open a brokerage account and buy the shares there, then turn on dividend reinvestment for them.

#8602. Which Debts Should You Pay Off First — Credit Cards or Student Loans?

Having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

If you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That said, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

You’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:

No matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data shows the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

To save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

Other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

The next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment plans.

If you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment plans and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

Once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

Then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

It’s important to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as quickly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

Finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

How much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete plan that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

Focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

In the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

#8601. I Bonds Pay 5.51% Now – Inflation Plus a 1.40% Rate That Lasts 30 Years

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

New I bonds earn 5.51% a year for their first six months. That’s inflation plus a 1.40% fixed rate. Your bond keeps that 1.40%, the highest since 2006, for 30 years. If you won’t need the money for a year, buy up to $10,000 at TreasuryDirect this year and another $10,000 from January through April.

You can’t control inflation, but the month you buy decides your fixed rate.

The inflation rate follows consumer prices. A new one takes effect every May 1 and Nov. 1, and your bond switches to the newest every six months, counted from the month you bought it. The fixed rate is set for each six-month buying window, then stays with your bond until it stops earning interest at 30 years.

For bonds bought from November 2026 through April 2027, Treasury set the fixed rate at 1.40%, up from 0.90%. That’s the highest since November 2006. The current inflation rate adds about 4.1% a year, for a total of 5.51%.

Say you buy a $10,000 I bond this November. At 5.51%, it earns about $275 in its first six months. After that, each new rate adds your 1.40% to the latest inflation rate. If inflation runs 3% a year, that comes to about 4.4%, and if inflation drops to zero, the bond still earns 1.40%. Either way, your bond earns about $50 a year more than a $10,000 bond bought in October, whose fixed rate is 0.90%.

You buy I bonds in an account at TreasuryDirect, the Treasury’s website, up to $10,000 per person each calendar year. A purchase this November or December counts toward 2026’s limit, so you can buy another $10,000 under 2027’s limit from January through April, at the same 1.40%. Interest counts from the first day of the month your purchase posts to your account, so buying late in the month costs you nothing.

Put in only money you can leave alone for at least a year. You can’t cash an I bond for 12 months, and cashing one before it’s five years old costs the last three months of interest.

Buy the first $10,000 by Dec. 31, then the second by April 30, before a new fixed rate takes effect on May 1.

#8600. Weekend Warm-Up: Keep It Burning

Keep it Burning: Making History on the Trango Towers follows Edu Marin as, along with his father and brother, he attempts a second free ascent of Pakistan’s Nameless Tower. He’s after the great Eternal Flame line, created by Wolfgang Gullich and Kurt Albert in 1989.

After failing the previous year, Edu Marin has returned to Eternal Flame with what he calls his dream team. That includes his 70-year-old father, Francisco “Novato” Marin, as well as his brother Alex. Neither has much experience with big-wall climbing or high altitude. However, as Edu explains, “I knew that they would stay until the end.”

It’s a strategy that paid off for the first people to complete a free ascent of Eternal Flame. Two decades after Gullich and Albert created the route, brothers Alex and Thomas Huber free climbed it. Both return for this film, sharing their experience from the first climb.

The three Marin climbers. Photo: Screenshot

They get to base camp at 4,200m and begin acclimatizing and preparing the logistical side of the climb. Managing the weather, the altitude, and the 1,200m of rope to fix adds another layer of difficulty. Then, when the team has settled in to begin the climb, an avalanche hits in the middle of the night.

Everyone emerges unharmed, though shaken. Novato recalls his fear that the avalanche would bury his sons, as they survey their dismantled camp. Everything needs to be dug up, but everything essential is still there, so the trio goes ahead and begins the climb.

They are making steady progress. But at the 6,000m Snow Ledge, they learn that a week of bad weather is heading right for them. While Alex and Novato head down to rest and wait out the storm from below, Edu sits tight.

“If you descend from the wall,” he argues, “you have to climb all the pitches again from the bottom.”

So instead he will sit on this 6,000m ledge, at below-freezing temperatures, for eight days. There’s a weather window that far out, and he plans to take it. This, Thomas Huber says, may be the hardest part of the project.

The sun comes out after 10 days of waiting. Reunited with his family, Edu leads the final ascent.

Edu on a technical pitch. Photo: Screenshot

The weather holds, and, encouraging each other as they ascend the last few meters, all three climbers reach the summit, with Edu completing the second-ever free climb. We see them on top, laughing and embracing, while final cutaway interviews with Novato and Edu discuss what it meant to complete the climb as a family.

“It’s a pleasure to share this sport, and to share it with my sons— there’s nothing better!” Novato says, smiling. “As long as my body allows me, I’ll keep going.”

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8598. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

First Highline on Trango Tower: On August 17, Lukas Irmler and Antonia Ruede-Passul of Germany completed the first-ever highline walk on Trango Towers in Pakistan’s Karakoram. They climbed Great Trango Tower to acclimatize before tackling Nameless Tower.

Setting up the 21m highline required fixed ropes and two summit ascents of Nameless Tower. The successful crossing saw Ruede-Passul break her own women’s highline altitude world record, previously set at 5,860m on Ojos de Salado in Chile, while Irmler surpassed 6,000m for the first time.

Following in the footsteps of Norway’s Great Adventurers: Steffen Skjottelvik set out to cross Canada, by foot, dog sled, and canoe, accompanied only by his beloved sled dogs. The Norwegian began his journey in 2023, but when one dog fell ill, he paused in the remote Cree community of Peawanuck. Here he found his home and a way of life that fitted him perfectly. He also fell in love with a local woman and became a second son to the community elders.

His original plan to travel by sled across the Hudson Bay coast changed after wolves killed one of his lead dogs. He decided to canoe the coastline in summer instead.

In 2025, he set off with his malamute Togo and a husky named Bay, facing polar bears, powerful tides, dense bogs, clouds of biting flies, and river crossings. On August 15, exhausted after weeks of difficult travel, Steffen could finally see his endpoint — the town of York Factory across the Hayes River. All he had to do was cross it. Togo survived and made it to shore, but Steffen’s body was found downstream 10 days later.

Where Was ‘Tenzing’ Filmed? Apple TV’s Tenzing recreates the historic 1953 first ascent of Everest, this time with Sherpa Tenzing Norgay at the center of the story. The filmmakers used real alpine environments across Nepal and New Zealand rather than green screens.

Nepal provided locations for Tenzing’s early life in the Lower Mustang, as well as the scenes in Darjeeling, Kathmandu, and Everest Base Camp. New Zealand’s Southern Alps, particularly the Aoraki region, doubled for Everest’s glaciers and icefalls, with the Darwin Icefall standing in for the notorious Khumbu Icefall.

Photographer Encounters Magnificent White Stag: Wildlife photographer Brian Johnston has captured incredible images of a rare white stag, believed to be an albino red deer. Johnston and a friend spotted the stag one windy morning during the rutting season, but it detected them and ran off.

Returning the following day, they found it asleep in a field, apparently exhausted after a night of rutting activity. Eventually, it stood up, giving Johnston the opportunity to photograph it.

Shark Attack Survivor Recounts Losing His Leg While Surfing: Australian firefighter and surfer Mel Ismail was surfing at Glenfield Beach on Australia’s west coast on September 14, when he was attacked by a shark. Sitting beyond the breaking waves, watching a pod of dolphins, Ismail initially thought a dolphin had bumped into his leg. Suddenly, he was dragged underwater and realized what was happening.

He desperately tried to push his fingers into the shark’s large black eye, and it released him. Ismail was bleeding heavily but managed to catch a wave toward shore. Another surfer spotted him and helped him onto the beach. Despite losing his leg below the knee, Ismail is determined to return to the water and start bodyboarding as soon as he can.

Canoe Dig It: Sam Dunning discovered freestyle canoeing during the 2020 lockdown after seeing a video of master paddler Marc Ornstein performing an interpretive routine to music. Amazed by the combination of technical skill and on-water choreography, the New York-based actor and filmmaker began writing Canoe Dig It?, a mockumentary inspired by comedies such as This Is Spinal Tap.

Winning the paddling community’s support was not easy, but at a freestyle canoeing symposium in Ohio, Dunning eventually met Ornstein. Ornstein and his wife agreed to be stunt doubles for the film.

Into Thin Air: This is a good background to the stories we’ve done on Kalie McCrystal, the 38-year-old skyrunner who disappeared on the Matterhorn on September 1. She met a Polish climber on her ascent, and theirs is the last footage of her. It shows her climbing towards the 4,478m summit. Shortly afterward, she was spotted descending the Italian side. Then she vanished.

Mountain rescuers believe she fell between 4,100m and 4,250m, but cannot establish exactly where or in which direction she fell. Despite a thorough search, no clothing, blood, or remains have been found. Her mother and sister eventually accepted that she had died on the mountain.

Climber Awarded Carnegie Medal After Rescuing Hang Glider Pilot: Matthew Clark has been awarded the Carnegie Medal for rescuing a hang glider pilot who crashed into a cliff on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

Clark, a 24-year-old climber and paraglider, had launched from the same spot minutes apart. Clark had just landed when he heard the crash reported over his radio. Reaching the scene with other pilots, he found Parson suspended in his harness around 15m above the ground.

With no walkable route to him, Clark spotted a narrow chimney nearby and free soloed up it, reaching him in about five minutes. Clark cut Parson free, moved him to safer ground, dressed a gash on his knee, and waited with him until a helicopter team was able to extract him on a long line.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

Certificates of Deposit (CDs) work similarly to online savings accounts or money market accounts in terms of offering great returns with zero risk. The difference is, CDs “lock your money up” for a specified period of time. To access your funds before the term ends, you’ll have to pay a penalty.

Although CDs offer less liquidity than a regular checking account or savings account, you might get a higher rate of return with this financial product. This is especially true if you open a CD account with a longer timeline; for example, a 60-month CD instead of a 12-month CD.

According to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), national average CD rates range from 0.23% to 1.81% depending on the CD term, as of writing.

However, quite a few banks offer vastly superior CD rates to consumers who do their research. We compared dozens of banks and financial institutions to find the best CD rates today. If you’re on the hunt for a high-yield CD, start your search here.

If your goal is securing a superior short-term investment, the best CD rates are worth exploring. To help in your search, we compared many of the top financial institutions and online banks to find options with the most attractive rates and terms.

Explore and contrast the top certificates of deposit (CDs) rates based on the highest Annual Percentage Yield (APY), spanning various terms including 3-month, 6-month, 1-year, 2-year, and 5-year options.

Raisin (Save Better) partners with some of the top banks in the U.S. for the highest rates on CDs. Check below for the current rates.

The banks below made our ranking due to the interest rates they offer and other features.

There are a few factors to consider when choosing where to open a certificate of deposit. These include whether you want to open your CD in person or online, the rates and terms that apply, and the fees required to access your money early.

The following reviews explain the CD rates for each of the top banks we profile and other details you should know.

PNC Bank offers a variety of popular banking products, including certificates of deposit. Its CDs don’t require any monthly maintenance fees, and you can monitor your account at any time online or with the BBVA mobile banking app.

CD terms range from 7 days to up to 10 years, and CDs with longer timelines pay higher CD rates. Note that penalties apply if you access your money early.

If you cash out your CD early, with a term of one year or less, you’ll pay $25 plus 1% of the amount withdrawn. If you cash out a CD with a longer-term early, you’ll pay $25 plus 3% of the amount you cash out.

CD Rates: Online CDs with terms from 11 months to 36 months currently pay up to 5.04% APY.

CIT Bank is known for its popular high-yield savings account, known as Savings Builder, but it also offers an array of CDs with excellent terms. Its 11-month, no-penalty CD stands out since it offers an excellent return rate. There are also no penalties if you need to access your money early.

CIT Bank also offers term CDs with various other lengths, as well as jumbo CDs for deposits of $100,000 or more. None of its CDs come with account opening fees or account maintenance fees.

CD Rates: CIT Bank currently pays from 0.30% to 3.50% APY on their CDs, depending on the term you choose. Top rates are offered on their 18 month CDs, which pay out 3.00% APY, respectively. With Discover, you can open a CD that lasts anywhere from three months to 120 months. There are no fees to open a CD, including account opening fees or maintenance fees.

Discover also stands out due to the reasonable penalties it charges if you need to access your money early. CDs with a term of less than one year, incur a penalty at three months of simple interest. For a CD that lasts one to four years, the penalty for cashing out early is just six months of simple interest.

CD Rates: The 18-month CD is most rewarding, currently offering 4.00% APY. If you’re willing to part ways with your funds for just 24 months, you can earn a rate of 4.10% APY.

Marcus by Goldman Sachs is a popular online bank for personal loans and high-yield savings accounts, yet it also offers rewarding CDs. Terms for its CDs range from seven months to six years, with a minimum $500 deposit to get started.

Marcus by Goldman Sachs even offers a 10-day guarantee that says you can move your rate up if the advertised rates on the CD you purchased increase within 10 days.

CD Rates: Some of the best CD rates from Marcus by Goldman Sachs are for its 9-month CDs, which currently pay 4.30% APY. Marcus by Goldman Sachs also offers limited-time CD rate promotions, like 4.40% on an 18-month CD.
