#8482. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

The Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

Mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8476. Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

“This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he said: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”

Through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby

While serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at New York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby showed nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

He gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The New York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”

The first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

After making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

In March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The New York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”

They made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby

Russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

The years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

When visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby

The distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

The arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

He lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:

I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

While Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

When his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

They later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”

In various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

“The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”

He has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

At the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa issues and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a new plan. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

Back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

The remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

He made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next issue. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

Karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube

As he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

Still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a plan for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

The crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

After 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The New York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he said. “It’s about to abruptly end.”

He is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

One big question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

Karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube

It might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

With just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

Then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

Now that he has to confront a new question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8471. Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

The second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

No cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

The climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:

We know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to new conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

The new snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:

It is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

On Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

So far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

A high camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Xenia Shanta

#8466. Te Araroa day 14: Finally back on some track

I got up fairly slowly and left at around 8am. The trail notes mentioned being able to walk on some farm tracks to skip a bit of road walking, so I headed off. It wasn’t very clear where I was supposed to go, but I found my way back to the road and started walking along. That is, until something made me think of my groundsheet. I had hung it over a gate when I was packing up, and I suddenly didn’t remember picking it up. I checked my bag and it wasn’t there. So I turned around and started heading back. This did not put me in a fantastic mood! Luckily I hadn’t gone too far, although realistically I wouldn’t have gone back for it if I’d gone a long way. It’s just a sheet of plastic!

By the time I had angrily marched back to the campsite and picked up my groundsheet, I was also hungry. So I had a snack of some crackers with mayo, which felt like a real hiker snack! Eventually I was ready to leave, again, at around 9am. I plugged my podcast in and hit the road. It wasn’t rainy, but was very muggy again, and the road was up and down but not as hilly as the previous day.

A highlight of this road walk was all the horses I saw. Those that know me, know that I’m a horse girl at heart! Some of the horses were very friendly, others less so. While I was trying to persuade some shy horses to talk to me, some tourists drove past and asked me about my trip. The woman wanted to tell me I was very brave for travelling alone. I told her New Zealand is a pretty safe country to travel in. Of course, nowhere is without its risks, but I’ve really never felt uncomfortable alone here – although in general, I’ve never been particularly worried about being a woman alone.

This cheeky guy was very keen to eat my bag!

Finally, it was lunchtime and I had just reached Helena Bay. I decided to pop down the road to the beach and see if there was a nicer lunchspot than a roadside ditch. And there was! A bench, a bin and a nice view made for an excellent lunch spot. Hikers really are simple folk, and this made my day.

A short walk up a hill later, and I was finally getting back on some actual track! The Helena Ridge track had clearly had work done fairly recently, but a number of large slips had knocked out sections of track. They were easily passable though, and the track went steadily up with some steeper sections of steps. I huffed and puffed my way to the top (mostly irritation at the number of steps – they’re so annoying!) and was pleased to find a nice bench at the top, well positioned to take in the view.

The track wound through the bush for quite a while, going up a whole lot more steps. At one point I started to see a hiker ahead, and thought it might be someone I’d met at The Farm the previous night. But it turned out to be a hiker called Graham, who was at The Farm but who I didn’t meet. He made his own tent, which is pretty cool! We walked together up the rest of the hill and came out into a grassy field. I was planning to stay at a free campsite a bit later, which might or might not have water. I had seen a comment on the TA app about a tap on the way out of this field, so I found it and Graham and I both filled up. He was going to head all the way to the holiday park at Whananaki, but I guess he needed water too. As I was finishing up, the farmer appeared in her Gator with her dog. She warned us that she’d just put some cows into a field we were about to walk through, and then just kept talking! She wished us a nice walk several times and then launched into another conversation.

Eventually we managed to escape, and headed on down the track. The cows the farmer had mentioned looked a little bit excitable, but we got through without problems. After a bit more up and down, we popped out at the ‘campsite’ where I would stay the night. There was a shelter, a water tank, and a rather lumpy, not very flat bit of ground. I had already booked the holiday park in Whananaki for the next day, otherwise I would have been sorely tempted to continue straight there. It was another 18km away, but it was only 3pm and I was feeling fairly fresh. Graham decided to have some food before continuing, and I was half wishing he would hurry up and leave so I could be alone, and half wishing he would stay so I wouldn’t be alone. Although I am very comfortable walking by myself in the daytime, I haven’t camped alone much at night. The camping spot had a bit of an eerie vibe, but I think that was mostly the mist.

An orange triangle being swallowed by a tree

I love whoever is building all these benches

I found a flat-ish spot for my tent, and had some snacks before making dinner. My dinner was pretty great, actually, and felt like ‘real’ food – pasta with veg, TVP, spices and tomato puree. Then I settled in my tent and listened to a podcast for a while before making myself go outside into the dark and scary night to pee and brush my teeth. I had read that there were possums about, and based on my experience with possums last time, I decided to put earplugs in so that at least they wouldn’t wake me up!

#8465. One Dead, Two Injured as Two Helicopters Crash Near Everest Base Camp

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

As shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from New Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

#8460. New Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health issues. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The new line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

This was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

#8459. In The Ogre’s Mouth — John Muir Trail Day 12

I woke up in my little tent spot nice and early, around 5:30 a.m., and then it took me two hours to get on the trail.  During that time the sun appeared to light the mountain on the opposite side of the valley.

Early morning view from my camp site. I needed Geologist Sam to explain the stripes in the rock…

This time the biggest delay was that the bottom of my tent was quite damp, so I spread it out to dry before packing it and heading on my way.

While I was doing all that, along came Sally who greeted me warmly and then walked on by.  Here’s a little more information about Sally that I learned the previous day:  she was born in Canton, and she works in medical research.  The rest I already reported.

By 7:30 a.m. I started off and immediately started down the infamous Golden Staircase.  I could see how it got its name.  Oh my gosh, it was just a straight down drop of short switchbacks back and forth, and back and forth, and back and forth, seemingly endlessly.  It was enough to make your ears pop from the altitude change.  Going down was bad enough, but I really felt sorry for the poor people trying to ascend it!  I could imagine how it might be demoralizing and exhausting as well.

It’s a little hard to see, but there is a trail going down that near-vertical descent!

Finally, I got to the bottom and eventually I even caught up with Sally.  We stopped for a water break together and then I went past her onto what was the nicest, cruisiest stretch since I started the John Muir Trail.

After the river’s steep drop coming down, the landscape leveled out and the trail mostly followed the gentle contour of the river heading due west.  As a smooth quality trail, it meant I could make very good time.  In the lower elevation the lizards reappeared, and I finally got some pictures of them.

As a child in Mexico City I bred lizards, so I have a special place in my heart for them!

I also  took a picture of a deer, some very large pine cones, as well as shots of several waterfalls.

It feels like somehow they know I am not a predator…

Lower elevations also brought much bigger pine cones.

Mostly, though, I kept a fast pace for about seven miles down the Palisade Creek valley to the river juncture with the Middle Fork Kings River, where the trail turned sharply north and started climbing again.

I reached that juncture at about 10:30 where I rested and had a snack.  Along with the food I took my last dose of antibiotics from the hospital.  I had to admit the medication had been highly effective, but not perfectly so.  I slept through the night now but still coughed occasionally.  I was easily 95% better though and grateful for it!

This was also the spot for errands including filtering water, filling my storage containers, and washing my socks and bandanas.  It was a little challenging to do this as the river was flowing swiftly, but I got the errands done.

My pack resting against a log. (I was resting too…)

As I took stock afterwards, however, I came up one sock liner short and assumed it had washed down the river.  Rather than accept its loss, I went back and looked for it.  To my pleasant surprise, I found I had unwittingly dropped it on the trail before washing.  So, I returned to wash it, then brought it back to its lonely mate.

Looking at those sock liners, I was disappointed.  In the past I considered them indestructible, but now I saw holes forming around the toes and elsewhere, apparently from chafing.  They were still worth using, but I realized they would not endure beyond the end of the hike at best.

Sally arrived at the juncture shortly before I departed.  Today it seemed we were tag-teaming more than we were leapfrogging, but I enjoyed a snack with her and directed her to the water collection site before hoisting my pack.

As I started going upriver, I realized I was at 8,000 feet, my lowest point so far on the JMT northbound route.  The next pass, John Muir Pass, would be almost 4,000 feet higher.  I resolved to try to get more than half of that elevation gain on this day, before making camp.

I was pretty sure I could identify the 10,000-foot contour.  In the Sierras, open fires are not allowed above 10,000 feet.  For this reason, it seemed every time we crossed that elevation there would be a sign flagging the change in fire status.  Most hikers would thereby know whether they were above or below 10,000 feet.

This shot was actually taken on a different day, but it captures what I was talking about, so I inserted it anyway.

As I ascended slowly, I eventually reached the turnoff to Bishop Pass, an indicator that I had gone ten miles already.  I was feeling pretty strong.   Without resting, I drank some water to prevent dehydration and pressed on.  It was a boost of confidence to reach the point I intended to stop, and to realize I still had energy for several miles more.

At a bridge over the stream I looked down and saw three little fishes swimming in an eddy of the stream.  I began to sing “Three little fishies in an itty bitty pool…”  You know that one?  First recorded in 1939, so maybe not.  At that moment a hiking couple arrived and no doubt thought I was completely insane singing to the fishes!

Two of the three little fishies… the third was camera-shy.  I am fairly confident they are Golden Trout!

I continued climbing and climbing through woods that changed as I went higher up.  For a while a number of thorny bushes lined the trail.  In my shorts this was uncomfortable; though they didn’t actually break the skin, they left many surface scratches.

I stopped to fill up my water bottle again at an ideal camp site.  While tempted to stay there, I decided it was still too early to pitch my tent.  Just as I was leaving, a guy came and asked if I’d take his picture on his phone.  I looked across the river and saw a stunning mountain.  “How cool,”  I thought, “I’ll crouch really low, aiming upward, and it will make a great picture with this giant crag looming behind him!”

That was not his intention at all.  It turned out I had not realized it, but I stopped at an iconic trail location.   The man moved toward a giant boulder, and then I saw it.  It was a face!  A face naturally created  by the geology of the place, but with a huge gaping ogre’s mouth.  In that yawning maw, people had placed a row of small triangular stones to represent teeth.  They added a couple on top of his head as silly little ears.

The man entered the “mouth” and lay down between the “teeth.”  He said his girlfriend back in France had taken her picture there several years before, so now I took his picture to send back to her.   Of course, having seen “The Thing” I had to ask him to reciprocate with a picture of me!  How funny that I almost left the site without even noticing it…

The forest was reduced to occasional scraggly trees as I hiked higher, passing more waterfalls as the slope became steeper.

Waterfall catching the sunlight, with the wildflowers in front? Lovely!

Shortly after passing the symbolic 10,000-foot sign (“No Fires!”) I came to a lush meadow.  It looked like a perfect camping area, and I found what seemed like an ideal spot off the trail.

I dropped my pack and turned off my AllTrails app and prepared to settle in.  Then I realized the meadow was flat and green and there were no logs or rocks for me to sit on.  I thought, “Let me wander around here a little nearby.  I’m sure I can find a nice big stone to carry over by my tent to sit on.”  Indeed, I found just such a stone.  But when I picked it up, I found under the stone was… toilet paper!  Ugh!

I put it back down in the same spot quickly and reassessed my decision.  Suddenly that place felt like bad karma, so I turned AllTrails back on again, shouldered my pack, and continued looking for a place to spend the night.

It was late afternoon already, and I worried that the camp sites higher up might all be full.  I decided to poll the descending southbound hikers passing me to find out what I might expect.  My question was simple and uniform:  “How many people did you encounter higher up who had already made camp there?”

The first person who came by answered, “One” and I was relieved.  But the second person who came along answered, “Six.”  I grew concerned.  Finally, the third downhill hikers were two women; they looked like mother and daughter.  To my question, the mother answered, “Fifteen, I think.”   Fifteen!  Then, to my relief, the daughter chimed in, “Oh no, I don’t think so, maybe five?”

This was a quasi-scientific experiment proving how totally unreliable we humans are at reporting anything.  Yet it left me with the same dilemma.  Then the daughter continued, “there’s a pretty site just up ahead and there still seemed to be room there.”

I looked on the AllTrails app, and it did show a spot nearby with four tent sites.   I figured, “Well, even if there are a couple of people there, I don’t mind sharing  and it will give me a little extra elevation and a little extra distance that I won’t have to take on tomorrow.”

Upward I trudged.  Soon, there was the spot with three tents already pitched, but space for a fourth about twenty yards apart from them.  The owners of the tents seemed to be friends, or maybe a family, as they had camp chairs and were all playing cards together.

Late afternoon arrival, with the sky still a deep blue!

I took my spot and pitched my tent, feeling very tired.  As I took off my trail runners and socks, I realized my feet were well beyond filthy.  I wanted a bed and a shower; not necessarily right away, but soon.

That was when I broke down and texted my wife on my Garmin.  It was something like:  “If you can get me a cabin or a room at the John Muir Ranch for day-after-tomorrow, I will be very grateful.  It is probably all booked up, but just in case, please give it a try.”

It was deep twilight by the time I soaked my dinner and dug my cathole.  I wolfed down my repast and called it a night.  It felt like it might prove to be a cold one.

#8456. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#8452. Te Araroa day 15: New friends and laundry drama

18km, free camp 307.5 to Whananaki Holiday Park

Using earplugs worked pretty well, and I slept decently. I poked my head out and saw that I was still in a cloud, but surprisingly, my tent didn’t have much condensation inside it. I went into the forest to do my business, and as I was emerging I heard the sound of running feet. A whole bunch of hunting dogs wearing radio collars came zooming out of the woods towards my tent, thankfully closely followed by some humans. The dogs started barking when they saw me, and the hunters called over to me that they were friendly – but I was happy to have a fence between them and me!

The weather was a bit mizzly with some heavier patches of rain, unsurprisingly since I was literally inside a cloud. The track went up and down a bit, and became a farm road before meeting a gravel road. After crossing that I went down an old ox track, which abruptly ended at a gateway and TA swung to the right over a stile into some bush. This track looked newly-marked, and wasn’t on the base maps yet – I guess there was probably some landowner dispute about the use of the original track, and it was re-routed to use the land beside it. It was a nice track through the forest though, and gradually I emerged down out of the cloud. Once again, the weather down there was hot and muggy. The track ran alongside some cow pastures and back and forth across a stream a few times before emerging at yet more tarmacked road, which I would be walking along for 7.5km. I put my headphones in and got stuck in.

The road was boring, but at least it wasn’t raining. After a while I reached the turning for a track that went alongside some more fields before reaching the Whananaki estuary. After a kilometre or so, I reached the back entrance of the holiday park in Whananaki. I had a booking for that night, but it was only 12 and I wanted to try to get lunch at the general store first. The accomodation options are limited along this stretch of trail, so I chose to have a short day and treat it as a semi-rest day where I would be able to do laundry and resupply a bit.

I found a path that headed towards the general store and the ‘town’. It went past the school, where there was a kapa haka festival on (Kapa haka is the traditional Māori performing art, probably best known from the All Blacks performing a haka before rugby games). I would have stopped to watch, but I was on a lunch mission!

Chips and caramel slice – the lunch of champions!

At the store, I got some chips and a caramel slice for lunch. So healthy! On the same site as the store and cafe was the local radio station, Whananaki FM. It was amusingly strap-lined ‘The greatest radio station in the world,’ in this tiny town (permanent population 330, according to Google). The radio was playing outside the store where I ate, and mentioned thunderstorms for the afternoon. It was quite nice at the time, so I didn’t think too much of it.

After my lunch, I headed round to the holiday park to check in. However, it turned out that the general store was also the office for the campsite, so I had to walk back to where I had just come from. Then I walked all the way back to the far end of the campsite to get set up at my spot. Once my tent was up, I gathered my laundry and got ready for a shower. The shower was coin operated, and $1 only got you 3 minutes. By the time I figured out where the ‘hot’ part of the dial was, my three minutes was almost up. So I had to go for another $1.

Then I tried to do laundry. I had bought a sachet of detergent when I checked in, so I found a machine, loaded it up, and tried to use the payment terminal. It refused to load. I tried again, and again. Nothing. I went out to the shop, and the staff there said it was because the wifi (which the machines need to accept payment) is Starlink, which doesn’t do well with cloud cover. Apparently it should come right in about 10 minutes. After 15 minutes, it still didn’t work and I went back to the shop. I must have seemed particularly upset, because they took pity on me and showed me where their ‘behind the scenes’ laundry was. That was nice of them, but I think perhaps it isn’t smart to have laundry machines that rely on wifi when the wifi is unreliable if it’s cloudy…

Once my laundry was finally underway, I went back to the shop once again to get a small resupply. Unsurprisingly for such a small place, the options were limited and expensive. But I had enough ‘proper’ food and really just needed a top-up of snacks. Aside from the laundry debacle, I liked this holiday park. They had humorous signage and the staff were helpful in my plight.

There was lots of this kind of amusing signage

Some rain started coming in towards mid-afternoon, and so did some other hikers. Harry, who I had met a couple of times, was the first person to arrive, followed by fellow Trek blogger Lindsey – who I was very happy to see back in action after her injury! – and Lucy, plus a number of people I hadn’t met yet. Cody, Eve, Sven, Issy and Riv all seemed nice and they had pretty much all decided to share some cheap but tiny cabins in view of the torrential rain and thunderstorms. I was sat in the kitchen charging stuff and working on some blog posts, and three seperate people offered me a beer that they had bought. Eventually I ventured outside to join them in the covered patio, where everyone was cooking dinner. They were a fun bunch and we had a good laugh. Sven had bought some postcards to send to various people back home, and one in particular was hilarious:

One of Sven’s postcards… note the chocolate fish, a Kiwi icon!

I went to bed a little later than usual, and with my brain running on overdrive from the unaccustomed social interaction. I lay awake for absolutely ages, watching the lightning and listening to podcasts to try to turn my brain off. But eventually, I slept.

#8451. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Plan B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team said that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet

There was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

Nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

The Spanish team sent us the video below summarizing the climb.

#8448. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#8445. Look What the Cat Dragged In

This is me. This is what I look like except 30 plus years older now.

A quick rundown about me. I was born in Japan and moved to the States with my family when I was… maybe three or four? We lived in a suburb of Chicago for a while and moved near Boulder, Colorado at the end of my freshman year of high school. During this larva stage of my life, I had the opportunity to go on some outdoor adventures via general curiosity in the woods, friends and family, and summer camp. From exploring mountains in the southwest to a 2 month canoe trip through Algonquin National Park, my love for the outdoors was baked into me from an early start.

The concept of thru-hiking was brought to my attention when I was in middle school. I was at a summer camp somewhere and we had just conducted a highly accurate stress test of a Nalgene bottle (back then, they were nigh indestructible). You see, what had happened was, we ran it over with an old truck on a dirt road.

The bottle flew by us at the speed of mach Jesus as it made contact with the tire and I had my first near-death experience via beheading.

We all laughed as we went searching for the bottle but came up empty handed. It was then that my camp counselor was reminded of a little event in his life that he referred to as his “thru-hike of the PCT”.

He regaled us with epic tales of adventure and exploration. The random side quests and people he met embedded stars in my 11 year old eyes that exist to this day (albeit, maybe a little less twinkle and shine these days). At that moment, I thought to myself, “I gotta do that some day”. Oddly enough, he wouldn’t be the first thru-hiker I’d meet. Every time someone told me about their thru-hike, it just reinforced the idea in my head that it’s something I want to do. Some day.

Anyway, after high school I enlisted in the Marines where I served for four years as a Reconnaissance Scout with combat deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan. The unit I was in was a little different from the average infantry unit in that we usually got sent outside the wire for 3-4 months at a time while living in some form of wilderness (no running water – so we can count the amount of showers we took on one hand over the course of each 9 month deployment). I suppose it was a natural progression of sorts in my outdoor journey. Not only did it prepare me for not showering for extended periods of time, but my official transcript from the military listed “Adventure” as one of the bullet points.

After I got out, I moved to Austin, Texas where I lived for a little over 15 years where I would drive myself to different parts of the state (and beyond) to go hiking, camping, and exploring (I even spent a year living in a van while going to school – that’s a whole ‘nother story). I also started volunteering with a disaster response non-profit where I got to help people in austere environments where I met some more thru-hikers. My most recent big boy job was working at Austin Community College teaching photojournalism in the Photography + Visual Media department.

I just recently moved to Las Vegas (not the one in New Mexico) after some events and revelations that I won’t get into detail here, however it’s important to note that there’s a little known fact about the area that helped me finalize my move out here.

What do you think of when you think of Vegas? Once you think of that, do you generally think, “hell yeah, let’s goooo!” or do you think “ew, no”? My assumption is that most people fall under one of these two categories.

I consider the next little fact as Vegas’ best kept secret… Are you ready?…

Oh? Did you not know that? Well, here’s some more info.

Surrounding this patch of desert is a range of mountains. Because of this unique mix of desert and mountain terrain, there’s a hidden/not so hidden outdoor community here. Do you see where I’m going with this?

I think it’s safe to say that most people hear Las Vegas and they think about casinos, strip clubs, and general shenanigans. However, that’s just the Strip. There’s a whole ass city here and surrounding this whole ass city is an expanse of wilderness waiting to be explored.

Well, some recent unfortunate events made me realize that after my current lease is over, I have the freedom to go do whatever I want. In addition, with the development of some health issues, my doctor basically told me that the most that can be done is to manage it. Fate has a funny way to kick you in the shins.

This was the signal for me to go do all of the physically demanding things I’ve wanted to do, while I still can – cause it ain’t getting any better.

There’s more to my story but that’s for another time.

Long story, long – I’m currently spending my time prepping for an AT thru hike attempt in 2028 by backpacking throughout the areas near me. The next year and some change will be spent going on shake downs, working out, learning, and seeing what works and doesn’t work for me. If any of this seemed interesting to you, stick around! I hope what I write might be entertaining or helpful to you.

And with that, I leave you to your regular scheduled programming.

#8443. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

While they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

Locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Company

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Company officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.
